title: Fraunhofer IIS Develops Automated X-Ray Analysis for Electric Vehicle Batteries - Batteries News
content:
Fraunhofer IIS Develops Automated X-Ray Analysis for Electric Vehicle Batteries
Fürth – The Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Circuits IIS has developed a software library for the automated analysis of 2D X-ray images of vehicle batteries as part of the AIR project. The technology enables the non-destructive assessment of mechanical abnormalities in battery systems, supporting both second-life applications and the safe handling of electric vehicles involved in accidents.
Reusing vehicle batteries can play an important role in conserving resources and lowering CO₂ emissions. Batteries that retain adequate performance and meet safety requirements can be repurposed for stationary second-life applications, ranging from residential energy storage to commercial and grid-scale storage systems.
Researchers at the Development Center X-ray Technology of Fraunhofer IIS and the Hochschule München , developed the AIR system to assess the mechanical integrity of used and accident-damaged high-voltage batteries without opening the battery pack or dismantling components. The system automatically detects cylindrical, prismatic, and pouch cells and identifies geometric irregularities that may indicate cell displacement, deformation, or swelling.
Mechanical Integrity as a Complement to State-of-Health Assessment
The electrical and electrochemical condition of a battery is typically assessed using the so-called State of Health (SoH). However, mechanical integrity is also an important consideration when deciding on battery reuse, transportation, or further diagnostic testing. Aging, vibrations, accidents, or deformation can affect battery cells and modules and may therefore have safety implications. To date, these aspects can only be assessed non-destructively to a limited extent in closed battery packs.
The AIR system addresses this challenge by enabling X-ray inspection of complete battery packs and providing additional information about their internal geometry and potential structural irregularities. The resulting X-ray findings form part of an overall assessment and do not replace electrical testing or case-specific safety evaluations.
Automated Analysis of 2D X-Ray Projections
The AIR system is designed as an X-ray scanning system. Depending on the inspection setup, either a battery pack or an entire vehicle is moved through the X-ray beam. The software developed as part of the project automatically analyzes the resulting 2D X-ray projections. In the test environment used, the evaluation of a battery pack took approximately five minutes. The actual total inspection time depends on several factors, including the size of the battery pack, the inspection setup, and the number of projections acquired.
Case Study: VW ID.3 Following a Frontal Collision
The performance of the AIR system was evaluated in a case study involving a VW ID.3. Prior to the investigation, the vehicle had been subjected to a frontal crash test under laboratory conditions at DEKRA. During the test, the ID.3 collided with the rear of a stationary VW Tiguan at a speed of 79 km/h.
Despite substantial deformation damage to the front section of the vehicle, the X-ray examination of the high-voltage battery installed in the vehicle’s underbody revealed no safety-critical structural irregularities visible in the analyzed projections.
The radiographic analysis of the nine battery modules revealed a uniform cell arrangement. Cell boundaries remained parallel in the X-ray projections examined, and no overlaps or bulging were detected. The image analysis software automatically identified the pouch cells and compared the curvature of selected cell edges. No critical deviations indicative of structural damage were observed.
The X-ray examination was complemented by a hazard assessment conducted in accordance with DEKRA guidelines, an evaluation of the Event Data Recorder (EDR) data, analysis of battery management system data, and additional electrical testing.
Based on the overall assessment, the high-voltage battery was classified as EUCAR Hazard Level 0, the lowest hazard category, and deemed suitable for continued use in this particular case.
Cylindrical Cells: Automated Detection of Severe Battery Deformation
The method was also tested on a traction battery containing cylindrical cells following a crash. The AIR system analyzed an X-ray top view of the battery pack and automatically determined the positions of the individual cells.
The analysis revealed a region that had undergone significant deformation due to mechanical loading. Compared with a reference dataset, several cells were visibly displaced. The automated position analysis detected these deviations and delineated the affected area. No indications of cell swelling were observed in the X-ray projections examined.
Despite the absence of indications of swelling, further use of this traction battery is not recommended due to the clearly identifiable mechanical deformation. The findings demonstrate that X-ray analysis can automatically identify damaged areas and thereby support decisions regarding further diagnostic testing, safe storage, transportation, or recycling.
Potential for Battery Reuse, Safety, and Resource Conservation
The results of the AIR project can help improve the assessment of used vehicle batteries for second-life applications. A more comprehensive evaluation of mechanical integrity can also support the handling of accident-damaged vehicles and batteries, for example during transportation, storage, or further diagnostic testing.
The technology may also be relevant for future inspection concepts in the context of periodic vehicle inspections for electric vehicles. Looking ahead, the planned Giant-Eye CT system at the Fraunhofer IIS Development Center X-ray Technology in Fürth is expected to further expand the possibilities for three-dimensional analysis of complete electric vehicles.

title: HPQ Silicon - French Army Technical Section (STAT) Awards Novacium a Contract to Supply High-Capacity Prototype Batteries for Tactical Radios - Batteries News
content:
HPQ Silicon – French Army Technical Section (STAT) Awards Novacium a Contract to Supply High-Capacity Prototype Batteries for Tactical Radios
Novacium was selected for its high-capacity GEN 3 and GEN 4 cylindrical cells, designed for high-capacity battery applications. The contract was awarded at the end of June 2026
MONTREAL, Canada
— HPQ Silicon Inc. (“HPQ” or the “Company”) (
TSX-V: HPQ
OTCQB: HPQFF
FRA: 8PY1
), is pleased to inform its shareholders that its strategic partner, NOVACIUM SAS, a French deep-tech company specializing in green engineering of materials for energy applications, has announced that the French Army Technical Section (“STAT”) awarded it a contract [1] at the end of June 2026 for the development and supply of high-capacity prototype batteries to be evaluated in tactical radios. For procedural reasons, the award could not be announced prior to today.
In August 2024, STAT, the French Army organization responsible for evaluating and qualifying equipment for land forces, contacted Novacium after reviewing published results from cells developed using its silicon-based anode material. The organization sought to evaluate the possibility of integrating Novacium’s cells into the batteries used in its tactical radios.
Following six months of internal development, Novacium’s teams developed two battery prototypes, which were provided to STAT in April 2025. The initial results were conclusive: with comparable form factors and interfaces, energy capacity increased by 23% compared with the reference battery.
Building on these results, in September 2025 Novacium met with France’s Directorate General of Armaments (DGA), Defence Innovation Agency (AID), and STAT to propose a work program to develop very high-capacity prototype batteries.
Several months of discussions followed to refine the program around an ambitious objective: significantly increasing, or potentially doubling, the energy capacity of tactical radio batteries without modifying existing connectors, chargers, or interfaces. This work resulted in a contract award to Novacium at the end of June 2026.
Selection Based on the Performance of Novacium’s High-Capacity Cells
Novacium was selected based on the performance of its very high-capacity GEN 3 and GEN 4 cylindrical cells, designed for high-capacity battery applications. This distinctive energy density made it possible to propose a solution capable of meeting STAT’s objective: significantly increasing the operating time of tactical radios without disrupting existing charging infrastructure, procedures or the logistics chain.
The contract provides for delivery in successive batches, structured around operational field feedback (RETEX). The first batch of prototypes will undergo an evaluation campaign under operational conditions, after which STAT and Novacium will jointly prepare a detailed RETEX. Lessons learned from this evaluation will guide design adjustments before production of a second batch that will better reflect a series-production configuration.
Dr. Jed Kraiem,
Ph.D., Chief Operating Officer of Novacium, said:
The award of this contract by STAT represents an important recognition of Novacium’s expertise in designing high-performance cells and batteries for demanding environments.
”We were selected because our GEN 3 and GEN 4 cells offer a distinctive energy density capable of meeting particularly demanding specifications. This program illustrates our strategy: applying our materials and battery expertise to critical defence and security applications,”
Potential Applications with Other Allied Forces
The expertise deployed under this program (high-capacity cell integration, battery management system adaptation and enclosure design) could be applied to other battery formats for tactical radios used by the armed forces of NATO member countries. A successful evaluation by STAT could serve as a technical reference to support this approach. However, each adaptation would remain subject to the relevant platform’s specific requirements, qualification testing, and separate procurement decisions.
Bernard Tourillon,
President and CEO of HPQ Silicon Inc., which serves as President of Novacium, said:
Novacium’s selection by the French Army’s technical organization responsible for equipment evaluation and qualification represents an important step in validating its expertise,
“If the evaluation phase confirms the expected performance, this program could become a relevant technical reference for presenting the solution to other allied forces with comparable requirements. For HPQ, every advance Novacium makes in the defence sector also strengthens the strategic value of our 36.8% interest in Novacium, as well as the potential to commercialize in North America the technologies covered by our licensing agreement.”
This contract is part of the continued development of Novacium’s activities in the defence and autonomous systems sectors. It follows the
August 19, 2026

Maersk has assumed direct management of PUMA's North American distribution network, taking operational control of three automated fulfilment centres across California, Arizona and Indiana.
Totalling 2.3 million square feet, the trio of facilities supports PUMA's wholesale partners, retail stores and
ecommerce channels
The partnership aims to boost fulfilment performance, maximise throughput speed and streamline regional product movement by combining robotics technology with integrated logistics expertise.
“This next phase of our partnership strengthens our ability to move products more efficiently across channels, improve responsiveness to changing demand and create greater value from the investments we've made in our US distribution infrastructure,” says Helmut Leibbrand, Senior Vice President of Supply Chain Management and Logistics Americas at PUMA.
Maersk-PUMA Partnership
Maersk now manages three automated PUMA distribution centres across California, Arizona and Indiana
The facilities total approximately 2.3 million square feet
The Torrance, California site will become Maersk's first multi-client AutoStore deployment in North America
Starting in 2027, Torrance will support additional brands with capacity for roughly 20 million units annually
Maersk operates more than 70 fulfilment facilities across North America, totalling 22.5 million square feet
Helmut Leibbrand, Senior Vice President of Supply Chain Management & Logistics Americas at PUMA. Credit: Helmut Leibbrandt via LinkedIn
Automating PUMA’s US distribution
Under the agreement, Maersk will operate three strategic locations equipped with AutoStore cube-based robotics.
AutoStore is an automated storage and retrieval system that combines proven cube-based
automation with advanced software
Inventory is stored within a compact grid and automatically retrieved by robots, bringing goods directly to employees at workstations for
picking and packing
In 2024, Deloitte surveyed 600 executives from large manufacturing companies with headquarters or operations in the US and 46% of respondents ranked process automation as the first or second priority for investment within the next two years.
Maersk says: “AutoStore helps improve speed, efficiency and workplace productivity while making better use of available warehouse space.

title: Climate Week NYC: Building Resilient Food Supply Chains
content:
Climate Week NYC: Building Resilient Food Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Leaders at Climate Week NYC explore the food supply chain. Credit: Unsplash
As ongoing climate events start impacting the food supply chain, leaders from Nestlé, Fair Trade and more convened at the Food Forum at Climate Week NYC
Food is an incredibly important resource, but it is also facing growing risk. Despite its critical nature, it can be overlooked when discussing climate action and the impact of climate change.
At Climate Week New York, senior leaders took to The Food Forum to explore the food supply chain and where businesses can
improve traceability
Speakers took part in a meaningful discussion, looking at where collaboration can make a difference.
A critical period
In recent years, external shocks have made their impact on food supply chains around the world. An increase in
extreme weather events
has put pressure on food production in various ways. Floods and unseasonable rainfall have resulted in food rot, crops have been ruined due to fires and drought and early harvests have been a result of higher temperatures.
The UK Government has declared food security as a national security issue, and other governments around the world are beginning to explore their own strategies.
The food supply chain covers agriculture, manufacturing, storage, distribution, wholesale and retail. As a highly interconnected system, it is incredibly complex, relying on time-sensitive deliveries, temperature-controlled storage, managing supply and demand and picking crops at the exact right time.
Agriculture timelines need to be planned years in advance, but recent weather disturbances have meant crops are ready to harvest earlier than expected, or yields are at a much lower intake. This has led to the growing disruption to food supply chains, with no signs of return to normal production.
As a result, business leaders around the world are looking to strengthen resilience and do their part to minimise environmental impact. Through improving traceability and reducing waste, leaders are working to make a food supply chain that lasts.
Key numbers
The agri-food sector supported 4.1 million jobs across Great Britain in 2025 (National Audit Office)
17% of GHG emissions come from agriculture
UK farmers are preparing for price increases of up to 70%
Nestle now sources 30% of its raw materials from farmers using regenerative agriculture practices
Nestle is committed to sourcing 50% of raw materials from regenerative agriculture practises by 2030
Fair Trade has mobilised more than US$1.4bn directly in fair trade premiums to community development funds in the past 30 years
75% of nitrous oxide emissions comes from agriculture
Responsible farming
The Food Forum at
Climate Week NYC
hosted leaders from a range of organisations over a series of panels. The recurring topics were traceability, expense and governmental policy.
Suzanne Sengelmann, CEO of Lundberg Family Farms, explained that moving to organic or
regenerative organic farming
is a risk for the farmer, as large-scale transitions can take more than three years before they are fully in place. At this time, there is a lack of profitability, as there is no official seal demonstrating these farmers are using these practises. As a result, they are enduring the added costs without seeing the benefit.
“For any farmer trying to start making the transition, it's expensive and a huge risk. So they need capital and they need secured demand,” Suzanne says.
Suzanne Sengelmann, CEO of Lundberg Family Farms
However, conversation on regenerative farming and other sustainable changes continues, exploring the long-term benefits of making this change. Though the initial cost is significantly higher, it is both better for the environment and for establishing long term resilience.
Yann Wyass, Global Head of Public Affairs at Nestlé looks at developing resilience from a global organisation’s perspective. Nestlé sells one billion products a day, around the world, showing the immense scale of the company.
“We are working very hard on regenerative agriculture and there are two main reasons for that,” he explains.
Yann Wyass, Global Head of Public Affairs at Nestlé
“The first reason is for climate resilience, but the second is for business resilience. Fertiliser price hikes, for example, have impacted a lot of farmers recently.
“We are very mindful that the transition from conventional or traditional farming to regenerative agriculture farming is and can be a risk to farmers. So we also combine what we do on Regen Ag with income, living income activities.”
Traceability is key to any claim. If you don't know where your food has come from, any claim you make about it is nonsense.
Chris Ninnes, CEO, Aquaculture Stewardship Council
Policy concerns
Despite this, many consumers and businesses around the world are limited. There are so many external factors which go into determining how people shop, or what they prioritise in their farming.
“You can't just say it's an individual consumer choice because
people's choices are shaped by policy
. They're shaped by how poor they are or the markets they have exposure to, the products that are marketed at them,” explains Paloma Lopez, Chief Sustainability and Communications Officer, North America Bel Group.
“There's no room to blame or shame individuals into making better choices for the planet. Our job is to figure out how we enable those consumer choices that are going to reshape our food production systems.”
Paloma Lopez, Chief Sustainability and Communications Officer, North America Bel Group
The world is currently facing a super El Niño, meaning food security is going to get worse in the approaching years. As a food supply chain is years in the making, the impact is a long-term issue.
This year, vulnerabilities in the food chain have been exposed, unveiling where organisations have dependencies on certain products or processes, or where they have crucial data points missing. The global food supply chain is at a crucial stage, with opportunities to become more domestic and more sustainable.
Traceability is crucial in this step. A leader can only make a positive impact with their supply chain, if they can track their supply chain. Every part needs to be visible, allowing leaders to fully understand their product and its impact.
The forum points to data visibility and technology as a core driver to change, but small organisations are limited without thoughtful policy and large-scale backing.
Climate change impacts
every part of the food system, from the growth of the product, to how it is delivered or the way the consumer receives the product. Resilience in this industry is not just about ensuring quantity, but also nutritional value and diversity of food sources.
Experts switched out on panels at the Food Forum at Climate Week. Credit: Climate Week
Key companies

HQ: Vevey, Switzerland
Global food and beverage leader with one billion products sold daily worldwide. The company sources 30% of raw materials from regenerative agriculture practices and aims for 50% by 2030, investing in farmer income programs and climate resilience initiatives across global supply chains.
Lundberg Family Farms
CEO: Suzanne Sengelmann
HQ: California, US
Organic rice producer pioneering regenerative agriculture transitions. The family-owned company focuses on supporting farmers through the costly three-year transition period to organic certification, providing both capital and secured demand commitments to reduce financial risk.

Global certification organization mobilizing US$1.4bn in community development funds over 30 years. The organization connects farmers with premium pricing structures and ensures ethical sourcing standards while supporting sustainable agricultural practices and farmer livelihoods.

Leading certification body for responsible aquaculture. The organization establishes traceability standards across seafood supply chains, ensuring environmental sustainability and social responsibility while enabling transparent claims verification for consumers and businesses.

Amazon has announced plans to invest more than US$100m in a new 585,000 square-foot
advanced manufacturing
facility in Greenwood, Indiana.
The investment will create 300
skilled manufacturing
and engineering jobs, with average salaries of nearly US$100,000 annually.
According to Amazon, it supports more than 27,000 direct jobs and 40,000 indirect jobs across the state, contributing more than US$35bn to Indiana's GDP.
“We're thrilled to bring 300 advanced manufacturing jobs to Greenwood, Indiana, and to continue investing in growth and opportunities across the state,” says Holly Sullivan, Vice President of Economic Development at Amazon. “This facility represents a significant investment in the Indianapolis community that will create jobs with a median salary well above the regional average.”
Amazon's Greenwood Investment
Amazon is investing more than US$100m in a new manufacturing facility in Greenwood, Indiana
The facility will create 300 skilled manufacturing and engineering jobs
Workers will earn an average salary of nearly US$100,000 per year
The 585,000-square-foot site is expected to launch by 2028
Amazon has invested more than US$40bn in Indiana since 2008
Holly Sullivan, VP of Economic Development at Amazon. Credit: Jacky Akbari via LinkedIn
Inside Amazon's Greenwood manufacturing plant
The facility will integrate advanced fabrication, robotic welding, automated powder coating and assembly capabilities under one roof, supported by AWS and
AI-powered

New roles will include CNC operators, welders, powder coating technicians, assemblers, manufacturing engineers, quality assurance specialists, controls engineers and programme managers.

The investment builds on nearly two decades of Amazon activity in Indiana, where the company has invested more than US$40bn since 2008.

robots are now deployed

have become central to that strategy because of the measurable returns they deliver.

title: Mars Advances Resilience and Traceability in Supply Chain
content:
Mars Advances Resilience and Traceability in Supply Chain
Prioritise Us
on Google
Mars is working to strengthen resilience in cocoa supply chains. Credit- Mars
Mars invests in traceability and climate-smart agriculture to strengthen cocoa supply chains and support responsible sourcing across global origins
Mars is working to build more
resilient cocoa supply chains
through its Cocoa for Generations strategy, which addresses sourcing standards, climate risk and the distribution of resources across its procurement network.
The company's 2025 Progress Report details investments in traceability systems, agroforestry distribution and supply chain mapping. Mars reports that suppliers sourced a volume of responsibly sourced cocoa equivalent to 98% of what the business required for Mars-branded products in 2025.
The business fell short of its full 2025 responsible sourcing targets but says it continues to fund initiatives designed to address interconnected supply chain challenges. As
Mars looks beyond 2025,
it is placing greater emphasis on professionalising cocoa farming and diversifying where and how cocoa is produced and sourced.
Supply chain traceability standards
Mars' Cocoa for Generations strategy uses third-party verification, farm mapping and supply chain traceability to support responsible production across its procurement network.
All responsibly sourced cocoa is required to be
deforestation and conversion-free
, according to Mars. The Responsibly Sourced Cocoa Programme applies verification processes intended to monitor compliance across the supply chain.
In West Africa, suppliers implemented child labour monitoring and remediation systems for all cocoa volume produced and purchased from participating farmers in 2025. Mars acknowledges that its use of mass balance means cocoa from compliant sources may be mixed with other cocoa during processing, storage and transportation.
The company cannot guarantee the origin of the cocoa in a specific product because of how mass balance functions in its supply chain. This could mean that Mars-branded products contain cocoa from sources outside the verified network, even when the company procures an equivalent volume from compliant suppliers.
"Our progress is important because the challenges facing the cocoa sector are interconnected. Farmer prosperity, productivity, climate resilience, forest protection, community well-being and long-term supply security must be addressed together," says Benjamin Guilbert, Global Senior Vice President, Mars Cocoa Enterprise, in Mars' Cocoa for Generations 2025 progress report.
"Meaningful progress requires collaboration with stakeholders in the cocoa sector, integrated solutions, sustained investment and a commitment to continuous learning and improvement."
Benjamin Guilbert, Global Senior Vice President, Cocoa Enterprise at Mars
Climate risk and tree distribution
Mars funded the distribution of more than five million trees in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana in 2025, supporting efforts to restore damaged land and improve biodiversity across cocoa-growing regions.
These initiatives aim to make cocoa farms more
resilient to climate change
Across Latin America, Mars launched its first climate-smart agriculture programme with suppliers in Ecuador, the Dominican Republic and Peru. The programme helps farmers improve soil health and crop yields while supporting land-use and emissions reduction objectives.
The company is working to expand regenerative farming approaches that can help protect ecosystems and strengthen the productivity of cocoa-growing landscapes. Mars states that its cocoa footprint has been reduced by approximately 1.5 million tonnes of CO₂e compared with its 2015 baseline.
"A global supply chain demands global effort," says Nupur Parikh, Global Senior Director, Cocoa Sustainability, Mars, in the report.
"Through programs that support cocoa farmers in origins across West Africa, Latin America and Southeast Asia, we're helping to advance climate-resilient practices, create more economic opportunities and secure the future of cocoa."
Nupur Parikh, Global Senior Director, Cocoa Sustainability, Mars
Cocoa for Generations
To date, 37 cocoa clones have been registered by the Mars Center for Cocoa Science with Brazil’s Ministry of Agriculture.
There were 14 modules available through the Grower Toolkit in 2025, covering four languages.
It’s stated that 28 weeks is the effective period of the lychee-based attractant developed to help monitor cocoa pod borer populations in Southeast Asia.
Approximately 1.5 million tonnes of CO₂e is Mars’ estimated reduction in its cocoa footprint compared with its 2015 baseline.
Technology and procurement improvements
Science, innovation and farmer capability-building form part of Mars' efforts to improve productivity and resilience across its supply chain.
The company has developed improved cocoa planting materials in Brazil and Indonesia, alongside research into disease-resistant varieties. Mars has also developed tools to help farmers identify crop diseases earlier in the production cycle.
Digital initiatives include AI-powered applications designed to detect cocoa diseases and assess bean quality. These tools help farmers and processing facilities identify issues and take corrective action before supply is affected.
Mars is developing integrated pest management approaches and tools that can help farmers prioritise non-chemical interventions, including pruning and the removal of infected cocoa pods. To date, 37 cocoa clones have been registered by the Mars Center for Cocoa Science with Brazil's Ministry of Agriculture.
Programmes like this encourage Mars to "strengthen the cocoa supply chain from the ground up", explains Srikanth Ramachandran, Vice President, Global Cocoa Category, Mars, in the report.
The main goals include "professionalising cocoa farms of all sizes" and ensuring supply chains are more resilient, according to Srikanth. Through its Grower Toolkit, the company is sharing farming knowledge and best practices across cocoa-growing origins.
There were 14 modules available through the Grower Toolkit in 2025, covering four languages. The toolkit supports more informed decisions and the adoption of practices intended to improve agricultural productivity and supply reliability.
It is stated that 28 weeks is the effective period of the lychee-based attractant developed to help monitor cocoa pod borer populations in Southeast Asia. This monitoring tool aims to reduce crop losses and protect supply volumes in the region.
Mars is working to strengthen the cocoa supply chain. Credit: Getty
Meaningful progress requires collaboration with stakeholders in the cocoa sector, integrated solutions, sustained investment and a commitment to continuous learning and improvement.
Benjamin Guilbert, Global Senior Vice President, Mars Cocoa Enterprise
Sourcing diversification and partnerships
Mars' strategy recognises the importance of economic resilience and financial inclusion in cocoa-growing regions, which could affect the stability of its supply base.
Through initiatives such as Women for Change and the Journey to Thrive Programme, the company supports household livelihoods and women's economic participation. These programmes combine agricultural support with community-level interventions, including savings and loans associations and professional farm services.
"Combining the technical knowledge Mars has developed over the years with
ofi's on the ground expertise
is key to enabling precision agriculture practices tailored to the needs of small and medium-sized farmers," explains David Sandoval, Program Coordinator at ofi.
"The Grower Toolkit program has allowed us to share our knowledge in good agricultural practices and sustainability in cocoa, providing the field staff practical tools and recommendations to continue supporting and motivating cocoa farmers to implement more responsible and efficient practices."
Mars intends to focus on professionalising cocoa farming, helping farmers improve productivity, strengthen farm management and build more reliable income streams. This could help stabilise supply volumes and reduce volatility in the procurement network.
The company plans to support the diversification of cocoa production and sourcing through climate-smart and regenerative approaches intended to improve soil health and protect biodiversity. Mars says these efforts are designed to strengthen the resilience of cocoa supply chains and reduce dependence on single-origin sourcing.
Looking forward, Mars is placing emphasis on geographical diversification and improved supply chain transparency. The business continues to
invest in traceability systems
, farmer training and climate adaptation measures across West Africa, Latin America and Southeast Asia.
Mars is emphasising geographical diversification. Credit: Mars
Partnering with Mars
Imperial College London
Mars joined Imperial Business Partners to collaborate with researchers on challenges including packaging, recycling, nutrition and agriculture, translating scientific research into practical applications.
Mars Petcare partnered with Calm to explore the relationship between pets and human wellbeing, launching a pet-inspired collection of Sleep Stories, meditations and mindfulness tools.
ADM, Mars Petcare and Royal Canin partnered to support regenerative agriculture across more than 100,000 US acres, incentivising farmers to adopt practices that improve soil health and resilience.
BVA - 2019
Mars Petcare and the British Veterinary Association partnered to explore pet obesity, examining nutrition, human behaviour and healthy body weight through research, awareness and education.
World Food Programme - 2015
Mars and the World Food Programme have collaborated since 2015 to strengthen food safety systems, train smallholder farmers and improve access to safe, nutritious food.
FAO - 2015
Mars and the Food and Agriculture Organization have collaborated since 2015 to strengthen food safety standards, improve mycotoxin management and address emerging food safety threats through science-based approaches.

title: Amazon & WEF: Innovation in Fashion Supply Chains
content:
Amazon & WEF: Innovation in Fashion Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
A cross-industry initiative has been launched to innovate fashion supply chains
In a cross-industry initiative, the Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition has been launched, bringing together Amazon, Stella McCartney and World Economic Forum
Fashion supply chains are vast, interconnected networks which include raw material sourcing, design and final sale. Along the way, manufacturing and distribution are involved, adding further complexities to the chain.
The fashion industry faces significant challenges, including
major traceability gaps
beyond Tier-1, resulting in labour malpractices and poor environmental solutions.
In order to make the industry more responsible, The Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition has been founded.
Supply chain collaboration
At present,
the fashion industry
accounts for 2-8% of global greenhouse gas emissions, as well as contributing to significant plastic use, clothing waste, pollution, water consumption and microplastics. Within leading fashion brands, more than 95% of GHG emissions are Scope 3, caused by fragmented supply chains with poor transparency.
As climate events become more widespread, organisations need to act in order to reduce their impact and develop sustainable solutions for a more resilient future.
In a cross-industry collaboration, The Climate Pledge, Amazon, Stella McCartney and Canopy have co-founded The Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition. The coalition has support from the World Economic Forum and supports more than 60 Climate Pledge signatories.
It is a mass collaborative coalition, including fashion brands, manufacturers, retailers and innovators.
The aim is to support each other and reach net-zero carbon by 2040. By integrating new financing models and tools such as the Fashion Coalition Lever Library, the coalition aims to scale the use of sustainable materials and manufacturing processes across the industry. In doing so, the fashion supply chain environmental impact should be significantly reduced.
"Transitions of this scale don't happen brand by brand, they happen when an industry moves together,” explains Nicole Rycroft, Founder and Executive Director of Canopy.
“By diversifying fashion's fibre basket with emerging Next Gen materials, this coalition builds more resilient supply chains, reduces sourcing risk and keeps vital forests standing.”
Nicole Rycroft, Founder and Executive Director of Canopy
Industry figures
The fashion industry produces 2-8% of global greenhouse gas emissions annually
Scope 3 emissions account for 95% of leading fashion brands' total carbon footprint
More than 60 Climate Pledge signatories receive support through the coalition
30+ brands and suppliers collaborated to build The Fashion Coalition Lever Library
92 million tonnes of textile waste is generated worldwide each year (UNEP, 2024)
Fashion supply chains operate across 60+ industries through coalition partnerships
Sustainability innovation
At present, the materials and processes that could make a positive impact are too fragmented, costly or too scarce to be able to be implemented at scale. The coalition, therefore, is working to target early innovation, making it a standard process in the industry.
“Making sustainable materials the default rather than the premium choice requires entire value chains to move together,” says Clemence Schmid, Head of Circular Economy Transformation & Director, Global Plastic Action Partnership at World Economic Forum.
“The Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition is designed to enable that alignment to ultimately increase the confidence that can unlock investment to scale. This is how we can accelerate adoption today, not a decade from now.”
Clemence Schmid, Head of Circular Economy Transformation & Director, Global Plastic Action Partnership at World Economic Forum
The coalition will be supporting development, commercialisation and adoption of more sustainable materials and processes. This includes using waste feedstocks in materials, as well as driving processes that reduce water use and emissions.
Through changing industry standards, the coalition aims to transform the industry.
"For over two decades, I've worked alongside innovators proving that fashion can be made differently. The solutions already exist. What's been missing is the industry-wide commitment to help them scale,” explains Stella McCartney, Founder and Creative Director at Stella McCartney.
“The Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition is about turning innovation into infrastructure, creating real demand for the next generation of materials and giving the pioneers a pathway from
breakthrough to industry standard
Stella McCartney, founder Stella McCartney
Cross-industry impact
The Climate Pledge was co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019 and has since grown to include more than 700 signatories across more than 60+ industries. Much of these industries have some relation with the fashion supply chain, creating a complex cross-sector network.
The coalition builds on a
model of collaboration
, with an industry that relies so heavily on a wealth of resources. Organisations across every part of the fashion supply chain are brought into this network, working towards the development of practical tools and lower-carbon supply chains, through innovative materials and technologies.
"Fashion has no shortage of ambition on sustainability,” states Kara Hurst, Chief Sustainability Officer at Amazon.
Kara Hurst, Chief Sustainability Officer at Amazon
“People are already looking for more sustainable options when they shop, and now the industry needs to deliver at scale. Through The Climate Pledge, we're bringing together more than 60
fashion and retail brands
, manufacturers, and innovators to help make that happen."
WEF is helping the coalition to develop blended financing mechanisms which will help unlock large-scale investments. As a result, it will be easier to make sustainable materials competitive and grow them to scale.
More than 30 brands and suppliers consulted on the development of the Fashion Coalition Lever Library – a network to help companies identify the solutions, innovators and materials which will have a strong impact on their supply chain.
The coalition demonstrates how networks can come together to make a difference, offering real-world evidence for environmental transformation.
Through this, the fashion industry is working in tandem to remove waste from its supply chain and minimise its negative impact on the environment.
This is how we can accelerate adoption today, not a decade from now.
Clemence Schmid, Head of Circular Economy Transformation & Director, Global Plastic Action Partnership at World Economic Forum
Key companies
CEO: Andy Jassy
HQ: Washington, US
Amazon is a multinational technology company founded by Jeff Bezos in 1994, initially as an online bookstore. It has evolved into the world's largest e-commerce platform, offering cloud computing services (AWS), streaming entertainment, and artificial intelligence solutions. Amazon also operates physical retail stores and has made significant investments in sustainable initiatives, including co-founding The Climate Pledge to achieve net-zero carbon emissions.

CEO: Tom Mendenhall

Stella McCartney is a British luxury fashion house founded in 2001 by designer Stella McCartney. The brand is renowned for pioneering sustainable and ethical practices in high fashion, never using leather, fur, feathers, or skin. McCartney emphasizes innovative materials, circular design, and transparency. The company partners with environmental organizations and uses regenerative agriculture practices, setting industry standards for responsible luxury fashion.
The Climate Pledge
The Climate Pledge is a commitment co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019, pledging to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2040—ten years ahead of the Paris Agreement. Signatories commit to regular reporting, carbon elimination strategies, and credible offset measures. The initiative encourages cross-industry collaboration, with hundreds of companies participating. It represents a business-led approach to combating climate change through measurable, accountable action.

The World Economic Forum is an international organization founded in 1971, headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. It brings together political, business, cultural, and societal leaders to shape global, regional, and industry agendas. Best known for its annual meeting in Davos, the WEF addresses critical issues including economic development, climate change, healthcare, and technology. It facilitates public-private cooperation and promotes stakeholder capitalism.

The organization collaborates with over 750 companies to develop forest-friendly supply chains, particularly in fashion, packaging, and publishing industries. Canopy's CanopyStyle initiative works with brands to eliminate ancient forest fiber from fabrics. Their innovative solutions include supporting Next Generation alternatives like agricultural residue-based materials.
Anna Sui

Anna Sui is an American fashion designer and brand founded in 1980, known for bohemian-inspired designs blending vintage Americana, rock-and-roll aesthetics, and global influences. Sui's distinctive style features bold prints, rich colors, and eclectic patterns. The brand has expanded to include cosmetics, accessories, and fragrances. Sui has received numerous accolades, including the CFDA Geoffrey Beene Lifetime Achievement Award, solidifying her iconic status.

title: Tesla ramps Optimus to hundreds a week, but the robots can't generalize
content:
Tesla Optimus
Fred Lambert
| Sep 25 2026 - 7:45 am PT
Tesla is now building several hundred Optimus humanoid robots per week at Fremont, roughly 10 times its Q2 output, according to a new report. But the robots coming off the line still can’t handle generalized tasks – limiting their usefulness.
The report also describes fragile hands, misaligned parts on the assembly line, and suppliers that can’t hold quality at volume. Those are the two problems that decide whether humanoid robots make money: generalization and reliability.
Hundreds of robots, mostly for Tesla
The Information reported this morning
(paywalled) that Tesla went from a few dozen Optimus units a week during small-batch testing in Q2 to several hundred a week in August. Managers are reportedly aiming for a continuous automated line capable of more than 1,000 robots a week by the end of the year, with an eventual target of about 20,000 a week.
That line lives where the Model S and Model X used to be built. Tesla ended production of its two flagship vehicles in early May and
converted the Fremont line to Optimus
, pulling workers and engineers from S/X, and dozens more from Model Y, onto the robot program.
So where are all these robots going? Mostly nowhere. According to the report, most units are used internally for testing, training, and data collection. The ones working inside Tesla’s factories are confined to tightly controlled, supervised areas, and they’re programmed for specific tasks rather than running as general-purpose machines.
And the V3 robots Tesla is building now aren’t even the version it plans to commercialize. That one still has to pass stricter durability and reliability thresholds.
The hands are the hard part
Musk has promised human-level dexterity for Optimus. Getting there at scale is proving painful.
Per The Information, the hand and forearm contain over 100 screws and small components that workers still assemble by hand. Fixtures on several stations, including hands, joints, and electronics testing, can’t consistently line up parts that are far smaller and tighter-tolerance than anything on a car. The result is more robots needing rework after coming off the line.
Durability is its own problem. Some of the hand’s touch sensors have had reliability issues, and Tesla’s fix is a replaceable “sensing glove” that it plans to add next year so it doesn’t have to swap the whole hand.
Then there’s the supply chain. Tesla relies on outside suppliers, many in China, for motors and the precision gears that drive the joints. Some of them can make good parts in prototype quantities but struggle to keep quality consistent at higher volume.
Days to learn a basic task
The bigger issue is the brain. Three people familiar with the system told The Information that Optimus’ AI can’t yet reliably handle a wide range of tasks, and that its behavior can be unpredictable in situations it hasn’t been trained on.
Tesla is trying to build a library of basic movements the robot can recombine for new jobs. But it still reportedly takes several days for Optimus to learn even basic tasks.
To feed the models, Tesla has over 500,000 hours of training data and wants to double that by year-end. It has moved much of its self-driving data annotation team to Optimus, hired dedicated data collectors wearing camera helmets and motion-capture suits, and set up training hubs in Colorado, Arizona, and Florida.
The plan for customers follows the same logic. Tesla reportedly intends to lease, not sell, Optimus to a short list of companies whose factories and warehouses look like its own, so the robots have an easier time adapting, and to use data from those deployments to improve the AI. That’s the FSD playbook: ship the hardware, collect the fleet data, and promise the software will catch up.
This is also a far cry from what Musk was saying last year. In January 2025, he said Tesla would build about 10,000 Optimus robots in 2025 and that “several thousand” would be doing useful work by year-end. A year later, he
admitted that zero Optimus robots were doing useful work at Tesla
. He also promised a V3 reveal by mid-2026. It’s late September, and that demo still hasn’t happened.
And competitors aren’t waiting.
XPeng started running an automated IRON humanoid production line
in Guangzhou this month, targeting commercial sales in 2027.
Electrek’s Take
We think humanoid robots will become a big new category of robots. But we also think they’ll be a small fraction of the overall robotics industry. For most jobs, a robot designed for that specific job, like a robotic arm on a line or a wheeled warehouse bot, will be several times more efficient than a robot shaped like a human. The humanoid’s only real advantage is that it can theoretically do anything in a space built for people.
That advantage only exists if two things happen. First, the AI needs to generalize. A humanoid that has to be trained for days on each task and kept in a fenced-off area is just an expensive, less efficient specialized robot. Nobody has cracked generalization yet, and it’s extremely hard to predict when anyone will. Second, the robot needs to be reliable enough over years of use to pay for itself. Touch sensors failing and 100+ hand-assembled parts per arm aren’t a great start.
Based on this report, Tesla has problems with both.
But it wouldn’t be the first time Tesla made big product decisions based on AI breakthroughs that haven’t happened yet. In 2016, it started telling customers every car it built had the hardware for full self-driving. It has since admitted HW3 cars will need an upgrade, and “Full Self-Driving” still requires supervision nearly a decade later. Now Tesla has killed the Model S and Model X to build a robot whose AI can’t do what the product needs it to do.
Maybe Tesla gets there. But the company is again betting its factory lines on a software timeline it can’t predict. How many times does that need to happen before investors start pricing it in?

title: Lexus' electric 3-row SUV makes its first public appearance
content:
Peter Johnson
| Sep 25 2026 - 6:53 am PT
The 2027
Lexus TZ
is the first purely electric three-row SUV from Toyota’s luxury brand. Ahead of its upcoming launch, the electric TZ was spotted driving in public for the first time.
When is Lexus launching the electric TZ?
We got our first look at the
new 2027 Lexus TZ
in May, an upscale sibling to the upcoming Toyota Highlander BEV.
It’s based on the same platform as the electric Highlander and will be available with two battery pack options: 76.96 kWh and 95.82 kWh, which Lexus said will deliver a driving range of up to 300 miles on a single charge.
Unlike Toyota’s 3-row SUV, all 2027 Lexus TZ models come with an “evolved” version of its DIRECT4 AWD system.
The dual-motor all-wheel drive (AWD) setup packs a combined 420 horsepower and enables it to tow up to 3,500 lbs. Drivers will be able to choose from five unique drive modes that will automatically optimize drive settings: normal, sport, eco, range, and rear comfort.
2027 Lexus TZ electric three-row SUV (Source: Lexus)
Although it uses the same platform as the Highlander EV, Lexus said the TZ will stand apart with its signature driving experience. In fact, Lexus claimed the electric TZ has the quietest cabin of any of its SUVs to date, with a fine-tuned suspension, dynamic rear steering, and a reinforced body structure.
Inside, the TZ features the latest Lexus Interface Multimedia system. The system now includes customizable apps and widgets, plus an updated “Hey Lexus” voice assistant.
The infotainment system now offers full-screen navigation and added EV charging functions, like EV Routing and an EV Range Map.
At 200.8″ long, 78.3″ wide, and 67.1″ tall, with a 120.1″ wheelbase, the Lexus TZ is about the size of other three-row EV SUVs, including the
Hyundai IONIQ 9
and Volvo EX90.
With charging speeds of up to 150 kW, the electric TZ can charge from 10% to 80% in about 35 minutes. It also has a NACS port, so drivers can charge at Tesla Superchargers without needing a separate adaptor.
The 2027 Lexus TZ is expected to go on sale in late 2026 or early 2027. With its official launch coming up, the electric SUV was spotted driving in Toronto while filming a commercial.
A few images and a video of the TZ were posted on the #Torontocarspotting Facebook group (via Rigun KG) on Thursday.
Lexus has yet to announce prices for the 2027 TZ. Given that the
2027 Toyota Highlander BEV
is expected to start in the mid-$50,000 range, the Lexus TZ will likely start in the mid-$60,000 range as a more upscale option.

title: Geely's AI fast charging 'heals' EV batteries for 20% more cycle life
content:
Geely says its new AI-powered fast charging system can reverse some of the battery damage caused by fast charging, using micro-pulse currents to add up to 20% more cycle life.
Charging a car in under 5 minutes is great, but not if it wears the battery out years early. Geely claims that its ‘Smart Charging’ addresses that and it is using something that sounds like sorcery.
A 2.25 MW charger was only half the story
Earlier this week, we reported that Geely one-upped BYD with a 2.2 MW charger capable of 4-minute EV charges. The full announcement came on Wednesday in Ningbo, and the fifth-generation Geely Smart Charging Station is rated at up to 2,250 kW peak.
Geely also shared real-world results. In testing, the battery used in the Lynk & Co 10 and Zeekr 001 went from 10% to 70% in 4 minutes 30 seconds, and from 10% to 97% in 8 minutes 40 seconds.
That’s a hair quicker than BYD. Its 1,500 kW Flash Charging network, now at over 10,000 stations, takes Blade Battery 2.0 from 10% to 70% in 5 minutes and to 97% in 9 minutes.
But Geely spent most of its presentation on something else: what all that power does to the battery.
Micro-pulses to undo fast-charging damage
The main way fast charging hurts a lithium-ion cell is lithium plating. Push current in too fast and some lithium ions pile up on the surface of the anode (the negative electrode) instead of slotting into it. That lithium stops cycling, and the pack slowly loses capacity.
Geely’s answer is what it calls “lithium-ion pulse restoration technology.” The system sends micro-pulse currents through the cells to “reactivate” the lithium ions that accumulated at the negative electrodes during repeated fast charging.
Combined with AI-managed charging, Geely claims this increases battery cycle life by 20%. The bullet points in its press release say “up to 20%,” so treat that as a best case.
There’s also a home charging component. Geely says it developed a low-rate charging strategy that “gradually” fixes degradation from repeated fast charging while you’re plugged in at home overnight.
So the idea is that you fast charge on road trips, and your slow charger at home cleans up after it.
AI that predicts heat 30 seconds ahead
The brain behind all of this is Xingrui PowerMind, an energy AI model Geely co-developed with Chinese AI startup StepFun. It coordinates the vehicle, battery, charger, cloud, grid, and the station’s energy storage system.
Most EVs today cut charging power once the pack is already hot. Geely says PowerMind looks up to 30 seconds into the future instead, forecasting where battery temperature is heading and dialing power down before it gets there. Every car and battery gets its own profile, with the AI constantly changing how much current goes in, how hard the cooling works, and how long the session runs.
The targets: an average battery temperature of 55°C during charging, and a peak under 65°C.
To hit those numbers at 2.25 MW, Geely added what it calls the industry’s first five-point liquid cooling system. It cools the station’s energy storage battery, the charging pile, the cable, the charging port, and the battery pack, so no single link in the chain becomes the bottleneck.
A 6C battery for cheaper EVs
Geely also listed two batteries. The Shendun Golden Battery, the one used in the Lynk & Co 10 and Zeekr 001 tests, supports a peak charging rate of 12C.
And the one that matters more for most buyers is the Next-Gen Ultra Short Blade Battery. It’s meant for Geely’s more affordable models. Thanks to laser welding Geely developed for the cell tabs and covers, the company says the pack generates 10% less heat while charging, and peak charging rate goes up to 6C.
If it holds up, that brings 10-minute-class charging to cars that don’t cost Zeekr money.
Electrek’s Take
Top comment by Beario
It is impressive that a company is even considering this as it is something that adds longevity to your car. That being said, it is equally impressive the scale at which companies in China continue to innovate and make the technology better. Long term dependability certainly inspires confidence in making a purchase. Being aware of these technologies being developed and constantly being improved overseas is a sobering reality check that here in the US we are not only getting further and further behind, but makes you wonder what is in store for consumers here from our automakers.
If you thought that battery and charging technology were plateauing, think again. The pulse restoration claim is the most interesting part of this announcement, and it straight up sounds like magic.
Lithium plating is real, and the fast charging arms race in China makes it a bigger problem every quarter. Automakers know it. Tesla has been limiting Supercharging speeds on packs with a high number of DC fast charges since 2017 to protect them. Geely trying to fix the problem instead of just throttling around it is the right approach.
And most EVs in the US still top out well below 350 kW. How long before an automaker here even needs to worry about this?

title: Green Water & Power powers up its 10,000th EV charger in just 3 years
content:
EV Charging
Jo Borrás
| Sep 25 2026 - 6:01 am PT
The developers and electricians at Green Water & Power are celebrating a significant EV charging milestone this month with the deployment and energization of its 10,000th electric vehicle charging port –
in just three years
Green Water & Power (GWP) and their hardware partners, Autel, started rolling out L2 chargers together nationwide in 2023. Earlier this month, the companies powered up their 10,000th charger. That’s a headline number – but the real story is just how quickly they got there: 10,000 chargers.
For those of you doing the math, that’s nearly 10 chargers going online each day, every day, including Sunday, Thanksgiving, Christmas, and New Years’, for three (3) solid years. And, for what it’s worth, they don’t seem to be slowing down.
“From the outset,
we designed our charging hardware and supporting software to deliver reliability and flexibility at scale
,” said Michelle Luo, CEO of Autel Energy. “GWP has demonstrated what that looks like in practice by consistently exceeding industry benchmarks across their entire network. This partnership shows how dependable technology and strong execution can accelerate EV adoption nationwide.”
Getting charging to work, and home
DCFC, by Green Water & Power.
Green Water & Power is currently contracted to install over 3,000 additional Level 2 chargers and more than 100 DC fast chargers (shown, above) in the coming months, with other projects in various stages of development.
To their credit, however, GWP is quick to point out that speed of deployment doesn’t mean much if the network isn’t reliable.  “Property owners and drivers don’t care about how many chargers we’ve installed,” explains Danny Gold, President of Green Water & Power. “
They care that the one in front of them works every time they need it
. That reliability is what’s made Autel Energy a great partner for us since day one, and it’s what let us scale into every vertical our customers operate in, from hotels and apartments to schools and hospitals.
We’re just getting started
The company claims its network has delivered a combined 16.6 million kWh to date, maintaining an average uptime of 99.72%
and displacing more than 22,000 metric tons of CO2 emissions

title: Tesla Semi finally enters volume production, 7 years behind schedule
content:
Tesla Semi
Fred Lambert
| Sep 25 2026 - 5:31 am PT
Image: Tesla
Tesla officially launched high-volume production of the Tesla Semi last night at its new dedicated factory in Nevada, a plant it says can build 50,000 electric trucks per year.
The Class 8 truck was unveiled in 2017 with production promised for 2019. Seven years later, Tesla says deliveries “start now,” and it detailed a heavily redesigned truck in a
13-post thread on X
A factory built only for Semi
Tesla held the launch event at the Semi factory next to Gigafactory Nevada in Sparks, where
the first truck came off the high-volume line back in April
According to Tesla, the plant covers 1.8 million square feet and builds every variant (Standard, Long Range, and a European spec) on the same line. Tesla called it “our first factory built for Semi.”
Tesla Semi factory in Nevada (Image: Tesla)
Tesla leaned hard on vertical integration. It says it stamps parts and builds the batteries, drive axles, high-voltage distribution, cooling modules, and even the seats in-house, while “most truck plants just assemble.” It also claims the first powder-coated Class 8 truck and one of its most automated battery lines to date.
“Vertical integration is the only real way to bring cost down,” Tesla wrote.
4680 cells, a cheaper motor, and electric steering
The truck itself has changed a lot since PepsiCo got the first hand-built units in late 2022. Tesla says it spent four years redesigning the Semi “for true volume.”
The biggest change is the battery. Tesla moved from 2170 cells to its in-house 4680 cells, which it says means “less battery mass & fewer kWh with no compromise on range.” Tesla didn’t give a new pack size. When it
released the final Semi specs in February
, it listed 325 miles for the Standard Range and 500 miles for the Long Range at 82,000 lbs, with consumption of 1.7 kWh per mile.
The Semi drive unit now uses a steel-caged rotor and a bar-wound stator shared with Cybertruck (Image: Tesla)
The drivetrain was reworked too. Tesla swapped the carbon-fiber-sleeved rotor for a steel-caged rotor that it says is cheaper, more reliable, and more efficient. The bar-wound stator is now shared with Cybertruck, a part Tesla already builds at volume.
Tesla also says Semi is the first heavy-duty truck with electric steering, which gets rid of the hydraulic pumps and fluids that leak and need servicing. And it’s upfront about why that matters beyond maintenance: it “lays the groundwork for future autonomy.”
Thermal management now runs through what Tesla calls a “Megamanifold,” a heat pump that handles cabin HVAC plus all powertrain heating and cooling. It’s the same thermal system Tesla uses in Cybercab.
Image: Tesla
Inside, there’s acoustic glass, a roll-down window, and a cabin you can stand up in. Tesla also automated parts of the pre-trip inspection and can generate electronic logs of when those checks were done. That’s a real quality-of-life feature for drivers.
Uptime, charging, and the diesel math
Tesla claims its Semi fleet has had over 98% uptime so far in 2026 and says the truck “requires almost no maintenance.”
On a Megacharger, Tesla says drivers get up to 60% of their range back in 30 minutes. It shared a map of Megacharger sites along major freight corridors, heavily concentrated in California, Texas, and the East Coast, with big gaps across the Mountain West and the Plains.
Tesla Megacharger sites along US freight routes (Image: Tesla)
Tesla’s economic pitch came down to one chart: fuel cost per mile for a diesel truck at 7 mpg versus a Semi at 1.7 kWh per mile using transportation electricity rates.
Fuel cost per mile: diesel at 7 mpg vs. Semi at 1.7 kWh/mi (Image: Tesla)
Based on Tesla’s chart, diesel has spiked back to roughly $0.80 per mile this year, while electricity has stayed in the $0.20 to $0.30 range. That gap is the whole business case, and it has widened in 2026.
Who’s buying
Deliveries start now, according to Tesla, which also says it will use Semis to haul its own freight.
Image: Tesla
Customer trucks at the event carried logos from PepsiCo, DHL, US Foods, ABF, Einride, IMC Logistics, and WattEV, among others. The big one came earlier this week:
the ZET SCALE alliance picked Tesla as primary supplier for 2,500 electric trucks
, an order that would nearly double the number of electric Class 8 trucks on US roads. That follows Einride’s 500-truck order in August.
Pricing is also a big advantage. Tesla hasn’t confirmed pricing since the event, but Electrek previously reported that Tesla has been
quoting $290,000 for the 500-mile Semi
and about $260,000 for the Standard Range. That’s up roughly 60% from the $180,000 Tesla advertised in 2017, but still about $145,000 below the average price of an electric Class 8 truck.
Electrek’s Take
As I have been saying for years, Tesla Semi is the last Tesla vehicle program that gets me excited, and despite the many delays, it is finally here.
The Semi is real, it’s in volume production, and on paper it’s the best electric Class 8 truck you can buy. It’s cheaper than the competition by six figures, and the efficiency claims have held up with fleets like PepsiCo.
Tesla can clearly build the trucks. Now it has to sell them, and the Megacharger network has to fill in fast enough outside California and Texas to make long-haul routes work. Diesel at $0.80 a mile helps a lot.
We’ll be watching the delivery numbers closely over the next few quarters. If Tesla ships 5,000 Semis in 2027, it’s a real business. If it ships 1,500, that factory is going to look awfully big.
If you’re following the shift to electric trucks, the same math that makes the Semi work (cheap electrons beating expensive fuel) applies at home too. title: EWS reports 14% higher winter wheat yield at Austrian agrivoltaic site - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Austrian agrivoltaics provider EWS has reported a 14% increase in winter wheat yield at its Sonnenfeld research site in Bruck an der Leitha compared with a control area without PV modules. The company attributes the result partly to shading and changes in the microclimate beneath its tracking PV arrays.
Petra Hannen,
Emiliano Bellini
25 Sep 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
According to EWS, soybeans and biodiversity strips at its Sonnenfeld Pischelsdorf site have developed well despite the summer drought.
Austrian agrivoltaics specialist EWS has reported a 14% increase in winter wheat yield at its Sonnenfeld research site in Bruck an der Leitha compared with a control area without PV modules. The company attributes the result partly to shading and changes in the microclimate beneath its tracking PV arrays.
The result was recorded in the site’s 12-meter-wide cultivation strips during the dry summer of 2026, according to EWS. The company said partial shading from the PV modules can provide some protection for crops and soil during periods of high temperatures and affect factors including soil moisture and temperature.
The Bruck an der Leitha facility, built in 2022, is a research and demonstration project developed with the support of the University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences Vienna (BOKU). The agrivoltaic array incorporates different row spacings to assess their impact on electricity and agricultural production. EWS said the movable module tables are installed at center-to-center distances of 8 meters, 11 meters and 14 meters in different research zones, corresponding to cultivation widths of 6 meters, 9 meters and 12 meters.
Earlier results indicate that crop response can vary with the spacing between module rows. In 2024, winter wheat yields in the 6-meter and 9-meter cultivation zones were close to those of the unshaded control area, while the 12-meter zone produced around 10% more yield, according to results published by EWS.
The company has now reported a 14% yield increase for winter wheat in the 12-meter cultivation strips in 2026 compared with the control area without PV modules. The result remains under evaluation, however. EWS said BOKU is analyzing this year’s winter wheat harvest and that the findings are expected to be incorporated into the research project’s final report, due by the end of 2026.
EWS noted that agricultural yields depend on multiple factors and that longer-term research is still needed to establish the effects of agrivoltaics. Site characteristics, crop type, weather conditions and soil compaction during construction can all influence results.
The system uses trackers that follow the sun during normal operation. For agricultural work, farmers can move the modules into a horizontal position. During harvesting, the module rows can also be tilted away from each other by up to 70 degrees to provide clearance for agricultural machinery. EWS says its tracker rows can reach heights of up to 2.8 meters.
The company is also operating an agrivoltaic facility in Pischelsdorf am Engelbach, Upper Austria. The 4.58 MW project allocates around 80% of its area to agriculture, 18% to biodiversity measures such as flower strips, bee pastures and fallow areas, and 2% to PV system components. Agricultural cultivation strips are 9 meters wide.
EWS said soybeans at the Pischelsdorf site developed well during the particularly dry summer of 2026, along with the site’s biodiversity areas. The company attributed this partly to protection from intense solar radiation provided by the elevated PV modules. It has not yet published soybean yield data, however, so the effect of the system on the harvest remains to be determined.

title: Solar panel waste silver turned into catalyst for carbon monoxide production - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
South Korean researchers have recovered high-purity silver from end-of-life silicon solar panels and used it to produce electrocatalysts for converting carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide. The recycled-silver electrode sustained CO production for more than 600 hours, with its rough surface helping to prevent electrolyzer flooding.
Lior Kahana
25 Sep 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Raw Materials
Silver powder is a component in the silver paste that is applied to wafers as a conductor.
Researchers in South Korea have developed a new method to upcycle high-purity silver nanoparticles recovered from end-of-life silicon solar panels into electrocatalysts for high-rate carbon monoxide (CO) production. CO is an important industrial feedstock used in the production of chemicals and fuels, including methanol, acetic acid and synthetic hydrocarbons.
The recovered silver formed a rough catalyst surface that helped prevent flooding inside the electrolyzer, allowing it to sustain CO production for more than 600 hours.
“This work highlights that upcycled photovoltaic waste can serve as a highly durable and scalable alternative to resource-intensive commercial catalysts, pushing forward the practical implementation of sustainable carbon dioxide (CO₂) conversion,” the academics said. “This work underscores the potential of integrating electronic waste valorization with electrocatalytic carbon utilization.”
The researchers collected end-of-life silicon solar panels and mechanically processed them using a commercial separation system operated by Reset Company. After removing the aluminum frames, tempered glass and backsheets, they heated the remaining solar cell fragments to 800 C to decompose the ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA) encapsulant.
They then immersed the fragments in nitric acid, dissolving the metals and separating the silicon residue. In a first alkaline treatment, they precipitated impurities including copper, aluminum and lead. A second alkaline treatment precipitated the silver as silver oxide.
The team then dispersed the silver oxide in ethanol with stearic acid and applied laser irradiation to reduce it to metallic silver nanoparticles. The researchers mixed the recovered particles with a Nafion ionomer solution and isopropanol before spray-coating the ink onto a carbon gas diffusion layer at 70 C.
Using the same preparation method and a target silver loading of 1 mg/cm², they fabricated a comparison electrode from commercial silver nanoparticles. Both electrodes were tested in a 10 cm² zero-gap membrane electrode assembly (MEA) electrolyzer, with a potassium bicarbonate solution circulating on the anode side and CO₂ supplied to the cathode.
The researchers used microscopy and chemical analyses to examine the particles’ size, shape, crystal structure and purity, and then compared the surfaces of the two coated electrodes. In the electrolyzer, they measured CO production and selectivity at increasing current densities and conducted extended tests to assess durability.
They also measured how strongly water droplets and CO₂ bubbles adhered to each electrode. Finally, they used a transparent electrolyzer to observe liquid entering the gas diffusion layers during operation, allowing them to compare the electrodes’ resistance to flooding.
“Physical characterizations and surface analyses revealed that the hydrometallurgical recovery coupled with laser photoreduction naturally creates a highly crystalline metallic Ag state with a unique, multi-scale nano-to-micro morphological distribution,” the researchers said. “While this hierarchical polydispersity induces a minor trade-off in the initial electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) compared to uniform commercial counterparts, it acts as a critical structural asset during high-rate MEA operations.”
According to the results, the end-of-life silver (EoL-Ag) gas diffusion electrode demonstrated high flooding tolerance, sustaining continuous, stable CO₂ electrolysis in a 10 cm² zero-gap cell for more than 600 hours at 100 mA/cm². It also operated for 55 hours at an industrially relevant current density of 200 mA/cm², while maintaining CO selectivity of around 95%.
The article “
Upcycling photovoltaic silver waste into hierarchically structured electrocatalysts for flooding-resistant zero-gap CO2-to-CO electrolysis
” was published in the
Journal of CO2 Utilization
Researchers from South Korea’s
Korea Institute of Science and Technology (KIST)
, RESET Company,
Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU)
Korea University of Science and Technology (UST)
Yonsei University
contributed to the study.
