title: Inclusive leadership: turning diverse perspectives into innovation and impact - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
At Solar & Storage Live UK 2026, Women in Solar+ Europe (WiSEu) explored the leadership behaviours that help diverse teams contribute, challenge ideas and drive innovation. A Solar+ Leaders panel extended the conversation to the trust and responsibility needed to deliver lasting impact.
pv magazine
25 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Solar and storage are advancing rapidly. But are the ways we lead people evolving at the same pace? That question brought industry leaders together for WiSEu and Solar+ panels at Solar & Storage Live UK.
The discussion around inclusion moved beyond whether people feel welcome. It examined whether they can influence decisions, contribute ideas and take ownership of solutions. For a sector that needs to attract talent, innovate and grow responsibly, inclusive leadership is a practical capability.
Belonging creates the conditions for contribution
“Belonging on its own just gets you a room where everyone feels welcome. It doesn’t get you the breakthrough,” said Liam Tattershall, Group CEO at Solarport. What moves a team from comfort to innovation, he argued, is whether people feel able to challenge each other and build on each other’s ideas.
At Solarport, cross-departmental “sandpit sessions” put real problems in front of people from every part of the business. Some of the company’s best breakthroughs have come from people who sit nowhere near the innovation team. Its suggestion scheme follows the same principle: every idea receives feedback, and the ideas taken forward are championed by the people who proposed them.
Tattershall also made the case for widening access to the industry. A sector growing this quickly cannot keep recruiting from the same small pool. It needs career changers, people entering through less conventional routes and people who have not previously seen someone like them in a leadership role.
Hollie Carek, General Manager UK and Head of Partner Experience at OpenSolar, questioned whether established ways of working are keeping pace with technological change. Top-down decisions, layers of approval and measuring people by hours rather than outcomes can all limit their ability to contribute. “We work in an industry that’s constantly pushing boundaries on technology, but I’m not sure we always challenge ourselves in the same way when it comes to how we lead people,” she said.
For Carek, empowerment means giving people room to act as well as permission to challenge. It also depends on everyday habits: inviting quieter voices into the discussion, rotating who leads meetings, asking “what are we missing?” and recognising the person behind an idea.
Make room for expertise at every level
Liz Cammack, Non-Executive Director at Solar Energy UK, cautioned against treating seniority as a measure of expertise, particularly as solar increasingly intersects with other sectors. “The role of an experienced leader should not always be to provide the answer,” she said. “Sometimes it is to ask the right questions, bring together the right people and create the conditions in which a better answer can emerge.”
Ruth Nash, Senior HR Business Partner and DEI Lead at NextEnergy Group, urged leaders to examine the quick assumptions that can prevent talent and ideas from being heard. She described how NextEnergy Group puts inclusion into practice through NEXTogether. The programme brings together belonging groups for women, neurodivergent colleagues and LGBTQ+ colleagues, while giving employees at every level a voice in shaping priorities. Senior leaders opened its first education sessions by sharing why each topic mattered to them personally.
“The biggest differentiator is authentic leadership sponsorship,” Nash said. “The organisations that succeed combine visible leadership commitment with genuine employee ownership. That’s when DEI becomes part of the culture rather than just a programme.”
That commitment is tested when projects face pressure. Tattershall warned that speed and cost can become reasons to set inclusive practices aside. When that happens repeatedly, people lose opportunities to contribute and develop as leaders. The effect reaches beyond a single project: the sector weakens the leadership pipeline it will need for future growth.
“Inclusive leadership is what turns diverse talent into collective intelligence,” said Carmen Madrid, founder of Women in Solar+ Europe and Solar+ Leaders, closing the panel. “When people can challenge decisions, contribute their expertise and see their ideas taken seriously, we create stronger teams and better solutions for the energy transition.”
The Solar+ Leaders panel the previous day took the conversation beyond the organisation, asking how leadership decisions shape the experiences of customers, communities and partners. It returned to a theme from the WiSEu discussion: better outcomes depend on whose perspectives are heard and how much influence those people have.
That responsibility cannot rest with a few individual champions. Stephen Rosser, Investment Director and UK Legal Counsel at NextEnergy Capital, described leadership as creating the conditions for change across organisations and the wider sector. “Our job as leaders is to create the environments, within and outside our organisations, where the change we’re driving becomes an inevitability,” he said.
For communities, having influence starts with being involved in how projects are developed. “The energy transition will be judged less by the gigawatts we build than by whether people believe it was done with them, rather than to them,” said Alessandra De Zottis, Head of Government and Regulatory Affairs at Sonnedix.
Public trust also depends on how the sector communicates as solar becomes a larger part of the power mix. Molly Morgan, Senior Market Analyst at SolarPower Europe, noted that solar has long enjoyed broad public support, but its growing visibility also makes it a greater target for misinformation and disinformation. Clearly communicating its benefits for the climate, energy costs and energy independence is a responsibility that comes with leadership.
“Our sector has the difficult task of helping Europe out of this crisis, standing out as a solution for governments, businesses and citizens, while ensuring strong support from the general public,” she said.
Gemma Buckley, General Counsel and Chief Corporate Officer at Solarport, brought a supplier’s perspective. She leads the company’s Legal, People and ESG teams and recently helped guide Solarport to become the first solar mounting systems and carport specialist to achieve B Corp certification.
For Buckley, the process demonstrated what it takes to turn stated values into decisions and accountability. It requires attention to the whole supply chain and the local economy, as well as honest questions about the gap between the industry’s sustainability commitments and the factors that drive purchasing decisions. “Leadership only counts when it becomes what you actually do, not what you say,” she said.
Leadership that gives others influence
Across the two panels, a common principle emerged: people need more than an invitation to participate. They need the opportunity to influence what happens next.
That applies to a team member whose idea challenges an established approach, and to a community whose experience should shape how a project is delivered. The energy transition will need technology and investment. Its long-term success will also depend on leaders who make space for expertise, share ownership and act on what they hear.

title: The Hydrogen Stream: Germany, Austria and Luxembourg launch €2.12 billion program for sustainable aviation fuel - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In other news, African green hydrogen projects secure new funding and Mauritania advances the Aman project. Moreover, Ansaldo Green Tech is expands electrolyzer manufacturing, as Toyota, Iveco and Hyster advances hydrogen-powered heavy-duty transport.
Sergio Matalucci
25 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Hydrogen
Utility-scale
Hydrogen-powered airplanes developed by Airbus
Germany, Austria and Luxembourg
have launched a dual-auction mechanism to support the European market ramp-up of renewable electricity-based sustainable aviation fuel (eSAF). The mechanism will bring producers and buyers together, with public subsidies covering the remaining price gap between supply and demand. Germany will provide up to €2 billion ($2.28 billion), while Austria and Luxembourg will each contribute up to €60 million. The supported eSAF volumes are expected to be marketed in the three countries in proportion to their respective funding contributions. The mechanism uses a double-auction model in which eSAF producers compete to offer fuel at the lowest price, while buyers bid for supplies on the demand side. An intermediary concludes longer-term contracts with producers and shorter-term agreements with buyers, with public funding covering the resulting price gap. This is designed to provide producers with the long-term revenue certainty needed to finance new eSAF plants while limiting subsidies through competitive bidding.
Mauritania’s
Ministry of Energy and Petroleum has signed an agreement with
CWP Global
for the development of the Aman green hydrogen project, establishing the long-term contractual framework for its next phases, as well as its fiscal, economic and development terms. CWP Global Chairman Mark Crandall said the project has reached the front-end engineering design (FEED) stage, with a final investment decision targeted before 2030.
African Development Bank Group (AfDB)
will provide $20 million in reimbursable grants to support four green hydrogen and low-carbon iron projects in Africa. Egypt’s Ra project will receive $3.55 million, Morocco’s Guelmim Green Hydrogen Valley $5.28 million, Namibia’s Hyphen project $5.93 million, and South Africa’s Saldanha Hydrogen DRI project $5.24 million. The AfDB said the four projects represent an estimated $23 billion in investment and include the equivalent of 20 GW of solar and wind generation capacity, 7 GW of electrolyzer capacity, and 2,950 MWh of battery energy storage capacity.
Ansaldo Green Tech
has completed a new production line for anion exchange membrane (AEM) electrolyzer stacks at its facility in Genoa, Italy. The company said the line has an annual production capacity of more than 300 MW. Its modular portfolio ranges from a 1 MW containerized system capable of producing about 500 kg of hydrogen per day to multi-megawatt systems for large-scale industrial applications.

title: India adds 50.6 GW of solar module and 9.7 GW of cell manufacturing capacity in 1H - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
As of June 2026, India’s cumulative solar module manufacturing capacity stood at 261.7 GW, while cell manufacturing capacity reached 36.6 GW.
Uma Gupta
25 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
solar cells
Premier Energies solar cell facility
India added 50.6 GW of solar module and 9.7 GW of cell manufacturing capacity in the first half (1H) of 2026, taking its cumulative solar module manufacturing capacity to 261.7 GW and cell manufacturing capacity to 36.6 GW as of June 2026, according to Mercom India’s recently released report, State of Solar PV Manufacturing in India 1H 2026.
As of the report’s release, cumulative module capacity under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) List-I stood at 225.5 GW, against nearly 35.5 GW of cumulative cell capacity under ALMM List-II.
“Domestic cell shortages have become the biggest near-term challenge for India’s solar market. Module capacity has expanded rapidly, but cell supply has not kept pace, tightening availability and pushing up prices for compliant modules and sharply slowing project activity. Many module manufacturers are struggling to maintain production because of limited domestic cell availability,” said Raj Prabhu, CEO at Mercom Capital Group.
Prabhu said that the installed cell capacity overstates actual availability, as new lines take months to reach stable commercial production. ALMM List-II has intensified the pressure by increasing dependence on domestic cell supply before enough capacity was commercially available.
TOPCon accounted for 80% of the total ALMM-listed module manufacturing capacity as of June 2026, followed by monocrystalline PERC/TOPCon at 11% and mono PERC at 4%. HJT accounted for 3%, while thin-film technology represented 2% of the total ALMM-listed capacity.
“Until commercially available cell supply catches up with demand, the entire industry will remain under pressure, with manufacturers facing production constraints and developers facing commissioning delays,” added Prabhu.
Gujarat remained the most favorable destination for solar module manufacturing, accounting for nearly 45% of the cumulative capacity as of June 2026. Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu followed with module production capacities of 26.1 GW and 23.4 GW.
Gujarat also held the largest annual solar cell production capacity at 37%. Tamil Nadu and Telangana were other top states, with capacities of 4.3 GW and 4.2 GW, respectively.
In 1H 2026, India’s imports of solar cells and modules increased 18% compared to 1H 2025. Cells accounted for 81% of total imports, while modules accounted for 19%.
The U.S. remained India’s largest solar export destination in 1H 2026, accounting for 92% of total exports.

title: Weaker monsoon lifts irradiance in western India as August storms dim the east - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In a new weekly update for
pv magazine
, Solcast, a DNV company, reports that northwestern and southern India and Pakistan recorded above-average solar irradiance during the 2026 summer monsoon, benefiting major PV-producing regions, while tropical depressions drove irradiance sharply below average across eastern and central India. Favorable solar conditions helped support Indian PV generation and electricity exports to Nepal after late-August floods damaged hydropower plants and other energy infrastructure there.
pv magazine
25 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Northwestern and southern India and Pakistan saw above-average solar irradiance during the 2026 summer monsoon, while August tropical depressions reduced irradiance in eastern and central India, according to analysis using the
Solcast API
. Fortunately, the majority of India’s utility-scale PV capacity is in the regions with favourable conditions. After late-August flood damage in Nepal, India began exporting electricity there, supported in part by Indian PV generation.
The monsoon arrived slowly in June and rainfall has been below average in the sunnier regions. Early June–September analysis, using forecasts out to the end of September, puts irradiance around 5% above the long-term average in those areas, whilst August saw up to 10% above average. The weaker monsoon is consistent with the strong El Niño that has developed throughout 2027. These effects are also influenced by a marginal positive Indian Ocean Dipole, an Indian Ocean temperature pattern that can counteract El Niño’s influence.
Accumulated irradiance at Jodhpur, near Rajasthan’s PV-producing areas, is provisionally tracking as the second-highest year since 2007. Bahawalpur, near solar installations in Pakistan’s Punjab province, is tracking at the top of its comparison years since 2007.
Eastern and central India followed a different course. Several tropical depressions, or low-pressure systems formed over the Bay of Bengal in August and moved northwest across land, carrying cloud and heavy rain. August irradiance in the affected areas was 20–30% below the monthly average. The provisional June–September estimate is around 10% below average across Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, eastern Madhya Pradesh and
Maharashtra.
Spot analysis of time-series data in impacted locations demonstrates the impact this has for local solar production, revealing the impacts of the onset of the monsoon. Seen below, Nagpur started above average after the late monsoon onset, but August rain pushed its seasonal total below average. Abikapur, in Chhattisgarh, is tracking toward its lowest accumulated summer-monsoon irradiance in the comparison record after an average start.
Less PV capacity is deployed in these eastern areas than in India’s main solar-producing regions in the northwest. The sharp local irradiance decline therefore had a more limited bearing on national PV production potential than the August irradiance data alone might suggest.
Late-August floods in Nepal and Tibet, attributed glacial collapse, damaged 12 hydropower plants, PV facilities and transmission lines. Nepal’s generating capacity fell by 10%. Normally an exporter of hydropower to India during the summer monsoon, Nepal instead began importing electricity from India after the damage. Indian PV generation supported those exports, alongside the favourable irradiance across India’s main solar-producing
regions.
produces these figures by tracking clouds and aerosols at 1-2km resolution globally, using satellite data and proprietary
AI/ML algorithms
. This data is used to drive irradiance models, enabling Solcast to calculate irradiance at high resolution, with typical bias of less than 2%, and also cloud-tracking forecasts. This data is used by more than 350 companies managing over 350 GW of solar assets globally.

title: China and U.S. module prices hold ahead of Golden Week and Section 232 price floors - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In a new weekly update for
pv magazine
, OPIS, a Dow Jones company, provides a quick look at the main price trends in the global PV industry.
25 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
China mainstream TOPCon modules held steady for another week as market liquidity remained thin ahead of China’s Golden Week holiday, with market participants reluctant to commit to transactions amid uncertainty over forward price direction toward year-end.
According to the OPIS Global Solar Markets Report released on Sept. 22, the Chinese Module Marker (CMM), the OPIS benchmark assessment for TOPCon modules below 645W from China, was unchanged at $0.108/W Free-On-Board (FOB) China.
Manufacturer offers remained wide-ranging, reflecting differing expectations for prices in the coming months. Industry participants also pointed to continued availability of lower-priced, less-efficient modules as a factor weighing on the overall module market.
Weak domestic installations since the start of the year have further pressured module demand and prices. China’s cumulative solar installations totaled 97.19 GW in January-August, down more than 57.9% from the same period in 2025. August additions totaled 11.04 GW, down 21.6% month-on-month.
Some industry participants said that weak domestic module demand has also made local module prices more sensitive to broader market fluctuations, prompting manufacturers to place emphasis on overseas sales. This shift in focus may explain the relative stability in export module prices, sources said.
Since the start of August, domestic ex-works (EXW) China mainstream TOPCon module prices have risen around 3.4%, while FOB China prices have remained flat.
The forward curve has also weakened over the past few months. OPIS assessed FOB China TOPCon module prices for Q1 2027 loading at a $0.02/W discount to spot prices this week, compared with a slight $0.01/W premium in late June.
In the U.S., imported module spot prices held steady as market participants continued to weigh the impact of Section 232 minimum import prices (MIPs), set to take effect Dec. 4.
Delivered duty paid (DDP) U.S. prices for TOPCon modules 645W and below were unchanged at $0.290/W, with quotes for Southeast Asian cargoes at $0.277/W and Indian cargoes at $0.332/W.
Quotes for U.S.-assembled TOPCon modules with imported cells, delivered on a domestic DDP U.S. basis, rose 0.63% to $0.321/W.
The Section 232 proclamation from early August continued to be reflected in the U.S. forward curve. DDP indications for TOPCon modules in the first two quarters of 2027 were assessed at $0.345/W, compared with $0.29/W in July.
Post-December supplier pricing remained unsettled, however, with a distributor saying the company had yet to receive firm prices as suppliers waited to see how competitors priced their products.
Uncertainty continued over whether the proclamation’s “first arm’s-length sale” rule would subject U.S.-assembled modules using imported cells to the $0.38/W module MIP. In OPIS’s Sept. 15 report, a source at a U.S. manufacturer questioned whether U.S. Customs and Border Protection would accept imported-cell transactions priced at the $0.22/W cell MIP plus the 15% tariff. If accepted, that treatment could allow U.S.-assembled modules to sell below the module MIP, the source said.
A policy source at a major supplier instead anticipated strict enforcement of the new price controls and argued that workarounds would undermine the mandate’s intent.
Views also differed on whether the enforcements would eliminate import demand. The distributor expected demand for imports to disappear, arguing that officials would raise tariff rates further if the announced controls failed to discourage imports.
The policy source, by contrast, believed imports could retain some cost competitiveness even if U.S. assemblers sold modules made with imported cells at $0.38/W, citing slim assembly margins.
For now, an early-stage project developer believed U.S. customers remained in contact with overseas suppliers and expected those discussions to continue while import prices stayed close to U.S.-assembled levels.
Beyond trade policy, the developer expected the industry to go on hiatus for a while after the final safe-harbor push for investment tax credit (ITC) eligibility, saying developers had stopped offering new projects when they no longer believed they could complete them before eligibility expired.
OPIS, a Dow Jones company, provides energy prices, news, data, and analysis on gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, LPG/NGL, coal, metals, and chemicals, as well as renewable fuels and environmental commodities. It acquired pricing data assets from Singapore Solar Exchange in 2022 and now publishes the
OPIS APAC Solar Weekly Report

title: Spain awards €265 million for 49.9 GWh of pumped hydro storage - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Pumped hydroelectric energy storage is advancing in Spain, with 11 projects backed by €265 million in public subsidies from a government program.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
25 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
The Cortes-La Muela pumped storage complex located on the Júcar River in Valencia, Spain
Spain has awarded €265 million ($302 million) to 11 pumped hydro energy storage projects totaling almost 4.1 GW / 49.9 GWh across two rounds of its Boralmac funding program.
The two rounds, resolved between 2024 and 2026, support new pumped hydro facilities as well as projects using existing infrastructure. The projects are spread across seven Spanish autonomous communities and are expected to be completed by 2035.
The first Boralmac round, resolved in July 2024, awarded the full €100 million available to four projects totaling almost 2 GW of turbine capacity and 28.85 GWh of storage.
The largest award, €44.9 million, went to the BOREAL project in Alcántara, Extremadura, for the new José María de Oriol II pumped hydro plant using the existing Alcántara II and Cedillo reservoirs.
Two projects in Castilla y León will make use of drainage water from abandoned mines. The Navaleo pumped hydro project in Torre del Bierzo received €35.3 million, while the Velilla del Río Carrión project in Palencia was awarded €10.7 million.
The fourth project, EcoEbre in Tarragona, received €9.1 million for a closed-loop pumped hydro facility between two reservoirs.
The original completion deadline for Boralmac 1 projects was the end of 2030. An amendment from the Institute for the Diversification and Saving of Energy (IDAE), approved in January 2026, allows the deadline to be extended to Dec. 31, 2035.
Boralmac 2 initially had a €90 million budget, but this was increased to €165 million following 16 applications seeking a combined €440 million in funding. Seven projects were ultimately selected, representing 2.07 GW of turbine capacity and 21.09 GWh of storage, against more than €755 million in eligible project costs.
The second-round projects include the 545 MW / 4.29 GWh Baells facility in Barcelona and the 354 MW / 4.74 GWh La Barca project in Asturias, which has the largest energy storage capacity among the seven projects.
Other awards went to the 440 MW / 3.52 GWh Meirama project in A Coruña, the 357 MW / 2.97 GWh Los Guajares project in Granada, the 247 MW / 3.81 GWh Grandas de Salime project in Asturias, and the 95 MW / 772 MWh Dehesa de Ganaderos project in Zaragoza.
The 33 MW / 991 MWh TORREALII project in Cáceres is the only Boralmac 2 project that will use existing infrastructure rather than construct a new pumped hydro plant.
All seven BORALMAC 2 projects must be completed by June 30, 2035. The second round is funded through the REPowerEU component of Spain’s Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan, while Boralmac 1 was funded separately under the plan’s electricity infrastructure, smart grids, flexibility and storage component.
IDAE said the projects were assessed on economic viability, technical characteristics, permitting maturity and their ability to support renewable integration and provide system services, including inertia and black-start capability.

title: German developer tests roe deer passages at solar park - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
German solar developer Südwerk has integrated roe deer passages into the perimeter fencing of its 20 MW Memmelsdorf solar park in Bavaria to preserve existing wildlife corridors. The company plans to consider similar measures in future projects following the experience gained at the site.
Petra Hannen
25 Sep 2026
Research & Development
Utility-scale
Roe deer passages are integrated into the fencing at several locations and are intended to allow roe deer to enter and leave the enclosed area without stress.
German solar developer Südwerk has integrated three dedicated roe deer passages into the perimeter fencing of a 20 MW solar park under construction in Memmelsdorf, Bavaria. The openings are designed to maintain existing wildlife corridors through the project site.
Südwerk said the idea originated with local hunters, who identified routes regularly used by roe deer in the area. German mounting system and solar infrastructure provider ZPV subsequently developed the fence design.
The passages are made primarily from standard components already used in solar park fencing and can be incorporated into the perimeter fence without custom fabrication.
The project’s ecological measures also include hedgerows, wildflower strips and extensively managed grassland, covering a combined area of around 15,600 square meters.
Südwerk said it plans to use the experience gained at Memmelsdorf in future projects and assess the feasibility of similar wildlife passages during the early planning stages.
The Memmelsdorf community solar park is nearing completion and is expected to begin commercial operations by spring 2027 at the latest. The ground-mounted array will have an installed capacity of 20 MW and occupy approximately 16.9 hectares.
A second construction phase is scheduled for autumn 2027 and is set to include a battery energy storage system. Südwerk has not disclosed the planned power or storage capacity of the battery system.

title: World's largest cluster of 18-MW wind turbines now fully operational
content: China has brought its first large offshore wind project built around 18-megawatt (MW) turbines into full operation, marking a major step in the country’s push toward higher-capacity offshore power generation.China General Nuclear Power Corporation (CGN) announced the milestone on Thursday for the Fanshi offshore wind power project in Yangjiang, Guangdong Province. The project is designed to supply electricity to the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area while supporting China’s expansion of large offshore wind farms.131 turbines deployed offshoreThe Fanshi project contains 131 wind turbines and is located about 50 miles (81 kilometers) offshore. Among them are 33 ultra-large turbines in the 18-MW class.The deployment makes the project the world’s largest large-scale cluster of offshore turbines using such a high single-unit capacity, according to CGN. The project demonstrates how larger turbines can increase electricity production while reducing the number of turbine positions required across an offshore site.Each 18-MW turbine has a rotor diameter of 958 feet (292 meters). Its swept area covers about 66,000 square meters, or roughly 16.3 acres. CGN compares that area with the size of nine standard soccer fields.The scale of the machines allows each turbine to produce substantial amounts of electricity from a single offshore position.One rotation can power a homeUnder full-load conditions, one rotation of an 18-MW turbine’s rotor can generate about 43 kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electricity. CGN says that amount is enough to cover the electricity needs of an ordinary household for about nine days.A single turbine can produce up to 56 million kWh of electricity annually, according to the company. Using larger turbines across the project can also reduce the number of offshore foundations and turbine sites needed for a given generation capacity.Fewer turbine positions can lower construction requirements for submarine cables and offshore foundations. It can also reduce the amount of sea area required for the project.6.6 billion kWh of annual clean powerOnce fully operational, the Fanshi project can send more than 6.6 billion kWh of clean electricity to the grid each year, CGN said.That output is equivalent to saving about 1.92 million metric tons of standard coal annually. The company estimates the project will also cut carbon dioxide emissions by about 5.1 million metric tons.Offshore wind has become an important part of China’s low-carbon energy transition because projects located near the coast can supply electricity close to major centers of consumption.“Offshore wind is a key driver of China’s low-carbon energy transition. Located near coastal load centers, offshore wind can supply clean power close to major energy consumption centers. It reduces fossil fuel dependence and helps energy-intensive regions achieve early carbon reduction,” said Sun Chuanwang, a professor at Xiamen University, as reported by Global Times.China expands offshore wind capacityChina’s wider wind power sector has also continued to expand. By the end of August, the country’s total installed power generation capacity reached 4.10 billion kilowatts, up 11.1 percent year over year, according to National Energy Administration data.Installed wind power capacity increased 19.6 percent to 693 million kilowatts during the same period.An industry report released in Shanghai on June 17 found that China accounted for 78 percent of newly grid-connected offshore wind capacity worldwide in 2025, according to CCTV News.The Fanshi project adds to that expansion while highlighting the industry’s move toward larger turbines and higher output from individual offshore installations.

title: New vertical quantum sensor probes materials in strong magnetic fields
content: Researchers at the University of Twente in the Netherlands have built a vertical quantum sensor that can measure nanoscale patterns in quantum materials and works in a magnetic field of 1 Tesla, which is 20,000 times stronger than that of the Earth. Recent advancements in our understanding of quantum technologies and the properties of quantum materials have led to rapid advancements in new applications. To further refine these applications and bring them into the real world, scientists need to understand further how currents and magnetic fields operate in these materials. Since quantum technologies run at nanoscales, scientists also need to build sensors that can work at these scales. A Superconducting QUantum Interface Device (SQUID) is an ultra-sensitive magnetometer that can measure extremely weak magnetic fields. However, magnetic fields weaken with distance, so the sensor must stay very close to the material to make measurements. A sensor lying flat in the plane of a quantum chip cannot capture details of the magnetic fields several micrometers away. So, a research team led by Hans Hilgenkamp, a professor of Applied Physics and Nanotechnology at the University of Twente, built a vertical sensor by putting it on a pyramid and bringing it as close to quantum chips as possible to see whether quantum materials do their work. How was the sensor built? Instead of building the pyramid, the research team hollowed it out from a slice of silicon. To do this, they used a liquid to etch out pits shaped like pyramids and placed a thin film of glass-like material on it. When the film is removed, the material remains only at the edges. The technique is known as corner lithography and leaves only a frame of extremely thin wires running along the edges of the pyramid. When the surrounding silicon is removed, the pyramid is left standing upright at the end of a thin arm. The researchers then added a layer of niobium, a superconducting metal, over the wires and then split the two constrictions on top into a ring using a beam of charged particles to complete the sensor. Conventionally, chips are made in flat planes, and while stacking is becoming more common, it can only be achieved layer by layer. The building of the quantum sensor shows that three-dimensional structures with working electronics inside them can also be made. Advantages of the sensorQuantum material research often takes place in areas with strong magnetic fields. However, this does not work well for a superconducting sensor since strong magnetic fields destroy its superconductivity, making them rather useless when you really need them. The pyramid sensor works reliably at 1 Tesla, which is 20,000 times stronger than the Earth’s magnetic field. Another advantage is that the sensor frame has four wires but needs only two for magnetic field measurements. The researchers use the other two tips for steer the sensor and tune it sensitivity during the scanning process. Much of the work in building a SQUID sensor has been done by hand so far. This research shows that building these sensors at scale from a silicon wafer, much like computer chips are made, is also now possible. The researchers added that hundreds of these sensors could be made in a single run, with nearly 90 percent of the chips being usable. The researchers published the findings in the journal Physical Review Applied.

title: California to house a 500-tonne annual output rare earth metal plant
content: Solcoa Industries has raised $75 million to build a commercial rare earth metalmaking plant in California, aiming to reduce the US reliance on China for materials used in electric vehicles, robotics, and defense systems.The financing will support construction of Solcoa One, a facility planned to begin operations in July 2027 with an annual production capacity of 500 tonnes of rare earth metals. The company says the plant will be among the largest rare earth metallization operations in the Western world.The funding includes $45 million in equity led by Bain Capital Ventures, with participation from Gigascale Capital, Long Journey, Felicis and other investors. Another $30 million comes from debt and equipment financing anchored by JPMorgan.A bottleneck in the rare earth supply chainRare earth metals are used to manufacture high-performance permanent magnets that help power electric vehicles, industrial robots, wind turbines and defense equipment. However, converting refined rare earth oxides into usable metals, a process known as metallization, remains a major bottleneck in the global supply chain.According to Solcoa, China controls approximately 95% of global rare earth metallization capacity. The company says conventional metalmaking methods are expensive, hazardous and difficult to permit, limiting the development of production facilities elsewhere.The issue is particularly significant for US defense suppliers. Under the Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement, restrictions already prohibit certain contractors from purchasing samarium-cobalt and neodymium-iron-boron magnets produced in China, Russia, Iran or North Korea.Beginning January 1, 2027, the restrictions are scheduled to extend to magnets containing rare earth materials mined, refined, separated, melted, or produced in those countries. That creates additional pressure on manufacturers to establish compliant supply chains for the metals used in high-performance magnets.A different approach to metalmakingFounded in 2025, Solcoa is developing an alternative to conventional molten-salt electrolysis, the process commonly used to convert rare earth oxides into metals.The company says its technology uses halide-free chemistries and modular reactors designed and manufactured at its Alameda, California, facility. According to Solcoa, the process is faster, consumes less energy, and costs less than legacy methods.The company also claims its approach produces no harmful emissions, including toxic fluoride gases and perfluorocarbons associated with conventional metallization. These performance and environmental claims have been made by Solcoa and have not been independently established in the supplied announcement.Rather than relying on a single large industrial facility, Solcoa says its modular approach lets be added production capacity incrementally, with individual reactors taking weeks to manufacture.The company reports that it has already scaled from a laboratory research reactor to producing more than 10 tonnes of magnet-grade metal annually. It says it is among the few companies outside China that can produce neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) and samarium metal, and is already shipping material from Alameda.Scaling to 500 tonnes annuallyThe new financing will fund construction and commissioning of Solcoa One, expand reactor manufacturing in Alameda, and hire across engineering and research teams. At its planned 500-tonne annual capacity, the facility could produce enough NdPr metal to supply magnets for up to one million electric vehicles, the company says.Solcoa CEO Hooman Reza Nezhad said the company intends to develop a fundamentally different metalmaking process rather than replicate China’s existing industrial methods.For US manufacturers, the challenge extends beyond mining and refining rare earths to establishing the intermediate processing capacity required to turn those materials into usable metals. Solcoa’s next milestone will be demonstrating that its existing production technology can operate at commercial scale. The company is targeting July 2027 for Solcoa One to begin operations, although the planned start date and production capacity remain company projections.

title: 8,157-ton nuclear attack submarine commences sea trials in UK
content: HMS Agamemnon, the Royal Navy’s newest nuclear-powered attack submarine, has left BAE Systems’ Barrow-in-Furness shipyard for the first time. She is heading to HM Naval Base Clyde in Scotland, where she will undergo trials and crew training before joining the operational fleet.The voyage comes more than 13 years after her keel was laid in July 2013. Although Agamemnon was commissioned in September 2025, she remained at the shipyard while work on her reactor plant and other systems continued.The submarine is the sixth of seven planned Astute-class boats for the Royal Navy.A long road to the first voyageWhen the submarine’s name was announced in 2013, the UK Ministry of Defence expected her to enter service in 2022. Her first departure from Barrow comes more than four years after that original target.Agamemnon was rolled out of the shipyard’s Devonshire Dock Hall in October 2024. King Charles III commissioned her into the Royal Navy on September 22, 2025, but the ceremony did not mark the end of testing at Barrow.Over the following year, work included testing and commissioning her reactor plant and completing other final tasks. The submarine conducted her first trim dive in October 2025, allowing her crew and builders to assess how she behaved in the water. She has now sailed from the shipyard one year and two days after her commissioning.Trials before operational serviceOnce Agamemnon reaches Faslane, she will begin an extensive programme of sea trials, weapons testing and crew training. Leaving the shipyard is a major milestone, but it does not mean the submarine is ready for operational deployments.HMS Anson, the previous Astute-class submarine, offers an indication of how long the process could take.Anson left Barrow on February 19, 2023, and subsequently underwent trials in UK waters and at the US Navy’s AUTEC test range in the Bahamas. She became fully operational around June 2024.A similar timetable would place Agamemnon’s operational readiness in the latter part of 2027. That remains an estimate: the Ministry of Defence does not disclose planned in-service dates for individual submarines, and Agamemnon’s own trials will determine her progress.A new boat amid a gap at seaAgamemnon’s departure follows a period in which no operational Royal Navy attack submarine was known to be underway. HMS Anson returned from an Indo-Pacific deployment to Devonport on May 27, 2026, and has remained alongside. That left a 120-day gap before Agamemnon sailed, although the new submarine is not yet operational.HMS Audacious, another Astute-class submarine, is nearing the end of a maintenance period at Devonport and is expected to return to sea in the near future.At 97 metres long and displacing 7,400 tonnes, Agamemnon carries Spearfish heavyweight torpedoes and Tomahawk land-attack cruise missiles. She is the sixth Royal Navy vessel named for Agamemnon, the legendary Greek king who commanded forces in the Trojan War.

title: US' South 8 begins making lithium batteries that work in extreme cold
content: South 8 Technologies has started operating a semi-automated battery cell manufacturing line at its facility in San Diego, California. The line will make cylindrical cells for defense and specialty applications that need reliable power in extreme cold.The expansion supports production of South 8’s ARCTIC AE35 18650 cell. The company says the line will support 5 MWh of annual production in 2027 as it scales capacity for customers including 3ME Technology and Galvion.The cell uses South 8’s LiGas liquefied gas electrolyte, which enables it to charge and discharge across a stated temperature range of −76°F (−60°C) to 140°F (60°C).Building cells for cold-weather equipmentBattery performance becomes a practical concern for equipment expected to work in freezing conditions. South 8 is positioning the AE35 for customers that build battery packs and platforms used in unmanned systems, communications equipment, remote sensing, and soldier power.The operational line gives the company a way to increase production of the cells while serving defense and specialty markets. South 8 identified 3ME Technology and Galvion as defense customers commercializing battery solutions that use its LiGas electrolyte. The company said the new line creates a path from cell qualification to production as it scales capacity through 2027. South 8 has not stated that the newly operational line is producing at that rate today.Domestic production and sourcingSouth 8 will produce both the AE35 cells and its proprietary electrolyte at its San Diego facility. Alongside the line’s launch, the company said it has established supplier agreements for key cell materials and components.Those agreements are intended to support a supply chain that avoids reliance on foreign entities of concern. For defense customers, the location of cell production and the sourcing of materials can matter alongside performance in the field.South 8 said its supply chain was selected with emerging sourcing rules in mind. It described the domestic line as a pathway toward meeting applicable National Defense Authorization Act requirements once those rules are finalized. The company did not claim that the cells have already been certified as compliant with finalized rules.Scaling for defense customers“Customers need battery cells that perform in extreme environments while also reducing supply chain risk,” said Rusty Heffner, South 8’s vice president of strategy.“South 8 is scaling production of the AE35 cell to address both needs. We provide the cold weather performance our customers require while building cells domestically with a supply chain that was selected to comply with the NDAA Section 842 rules,” he added.“We enhance the capability of our customers’ products and give them confidence that they will have a reliable domestic source of battery cells that meets emerging DOW regulations,” Heffener continued. The launch marks an operational manufacturing step for South 8, while its planned 2027 output remains ahead. Its customers can now work toward using domestically made AE35 cells in equipment designed for demanding cold-weather environments.

title: US firm hits 30 entangled logical qubits on its Sqale quantum computer
content: A Colorado-based company has announced a major milestone in quantum computing. Infleqtion’s Sqale quantum computer has demonstrated 30 entangled logical qubits using just 80 physical qubits. The 30-logical-qubit demonstration represents an important data point in the industry’s effort to move from isolated quantum experiments toward machines capable of executing increasingly long and reliable computations.Infleqtion becomes first neutral-atom quantum computing company to reach 30 logical qubitsThis achievement makes Infleqtion the first neutral-atom quantum computing company to reach 30 logical qubits on a commercial system. Infleqtion revealed that the breakthrough combines hardware and software co-design with an AI-assisted discovery that halves the physical gates needed for a key logical operation. By entangling 30 logical qubits in a single, coherent quantum state, Infleqtion has validated the core architecture of its Sqale hardware and Superstaq software, on its roadmap to deliver 100 logical qubits by 2028.“Getting 30 logical qubits to work together is hard, and our team has done it,” said Matt Kinsella, CEO of Infleqtion. “Co-design between our hardware and software enabled this demonstration with just 80 physical qubits. We’re moving quickly toward our target of 100 logical qubits in 2028, and we’re already developing applications with customers. The goal is to give them a quantum computer that can take on problems they can’t solve today.”Unlike fragile physical qubits, which suffer rapid calculation decay from environmental noise, logical qubits group multiple physical qubits together using software protocols to ensure computational stability and accuracy. Infleqtion’s achievement of 30 logical qubits was experimentally confirmed by a signal that is approximately 1000x stronger than underlying noise, according to a press release.Infleqtion has three customers for logical qubit circuits on the Sqale platform. Among them is the Wellcome Leap Quantum for Bio (Q4Bio) program, where Infleqtion pioneered and demonstrated on hardware a quantum neural network approach with training on GPU and inference on QPU for biomarker discovery. That work, first demonstrated at 12 logical qubits, extends directly into today’s result, as per the release.“Getting 30 logical qubits to work together is hard, and our team has done it,” said Matt Kinsella, CEO of Infleqtion. “Co-design between our hardware and software enabled this demonstration with just 80 physical qubits. We’re moving quickly toward our target of 100 logical qubits in 2028, and we’re already developing applications with customers. The goal is to give them a quantum computer that can take on problems they can’t solve today.”Breakthrough is powered by Infleqtion’s Superstaq quantum softwareThe company also revealed that the breakthrough is powered by Infleqtion’s Sqale QPU hardware and Superstaq quantum software platform, which unite individual qubit-addressing capabilities with dynamically reconfigurable atom arrays. This unique combination maintains all-to-all connectivity while minimizing the typical pitfalls of atom movement, including error accumulation, atom loss, and runtime delays.

title: China develops 360 feet high-performance recyclable wind turbine blade
content: A Chinese company has completed production of a 360 feet recyclable wind turbine blade. Developed by CRRC, the blade achieves a recovery rate exceeding 95% for key raw materials.The milestone marks a significant step toward the commercial-scale recycling of ultra-large wind turbine blades and provides a solution for managing blades at the end of their service life.Blade represents breakthrough in both materials and recycling technologyCRRC revealed that the blade represents a breakthrough in both materials and recycling technology. It uses a recyclable material system centered on a high-efficiency, debondable infusion resin. While fully meeting the demanding performance requirements for high strength, stiffness and fatigue life, the blade uses reversible chemical debonding technology to separate the resin efficiently from the reinforcing fibers. Once recovered, materials including the resin and fibers can be reused in wind equipment, automotive manufacturing, infrastructure construction and other high-value applications. This moves wind turbine blades beyond the traditional “single-use” model, enabling closed-loop recovery and high-value reuse of their constituent materials, according to CRRC.Recyclable blade system can support efforts to meet sustainabilityThe recyclable blade system can support customers’ efforts to meet international sustainability objectives and reporting obligations, including those under the EU’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD). It is also well suited to high-capacity offshore wind turbines and combines safety, environmental performance and cost-effectiveness. Together, these advantages strengthen CRRC’s position as it brings its offshore wind equipment to international markets and competes in the global renewable energy sector, according to a press release.CRRC claims its new blade uses a recyclable material system based on a high-efficiency, debondable infusion resin. The technology is designed to allow the resin to be separated from reinforcing fibres through reversible chemical debonding.This approach is significant because conventional wind-turbine blades rely heavily on composite materials that are engineered for strength and durability. Those characteristics make the blades suitable for decades of operation but can also make them difficult to dismantle and recycle once they reach the end of their useful lives.CRRC estimates that more than 470 GW of new onshore and offshore wind installations could be added in the coming years. At the same time, the company says that more than 30,000 wind turbines in China could be retired by 2030, representing approximately 44.73 GW of capacity and generating about 947,900 metric tons of wind-related solid waste.Last year, CRRC said it had developed China’s first TMT82 recyclable thermoset-resin blade. The company described the technology as using reversible chemical bonds to facilitate the depolymerization and separation of resin and fibres while maintaining the mechanical properties required for wind-turbine operation.The 360 feet blade is also aimed at the requirements of high-capacity offshore wind turbines.Offshore projects increasingly use larger turbines because greater rotor size can increase electricity generation from each installation. However, transporting, maintaining and eventually decommissioning components of this scale presents additional logistical and environmental challenges.

title: World's first isotope refinery project can transform fusion innovation
content: A London-based company is building the world’s first isotope refinery, which can enable the next era of medicine and fusion energy.For this, StandardX has raised £10m seed funding. The step is expected to radically increase production of the rare isotopes that will enable the next century of innovation in medicine and energy.“Isotopes underpin the next era of innovation across several key sectors, but all share the same constraints around supply,” said Richard Pearson, StandardX CEO.“Shortages are most acute in cancer medicine, already impacting patients today, and stalling progress in the development of next-generation treatments. This problem will only get worse, with new cancer cases projected to increase 67% by 2050. So we’re building the platform the world needs to address this.”Isotope refinery will turn chronic scarcity into reliable and abundant supplyIsotopes enabling a new generation of cancer treatments, particularly targeted alpha therapies, which attacks cancer directly whilst sparing the healthy tissue around tumours, are so scarce that clinical trials have been paused or delayed across the UK, Europe and beyond.StandardX’s isotope refinery will turn this chronic scarcity into a reliable and abundant supply. Its proprietary accelerator system replaces today’s patchwork of narrow, isotope-specific infrastructure. Deployable and built on a standard industrial footprint, each machine is capable of manufacturing the full isotope portfolio at commercial scale, supporting a distributed model of supply with production sited close to demand, according to a press release.Production will begin with isotopes for cancer diagnosis and therapy, servicing two markets: the supply hospitals rely on today, and the ones drug-makers need to invent tomorrow’s treatments, some of which are not commercially available at any scale today. StandardX will supply first isotopes to a medical research partner in 2027, as per the release.The company also revealed that the same accelerator platform will later scale to isotopes for other advanced industries, including tritium, the incredibly scarce fuel that fusion energy runs on: only 25kg of tritium exists globally today but tens of kilograms are needed to run just a single fusion power plant for a year. StandardX has already signed agreements with leading fusion developers to manufacture tritium to support their missions in bringing fusion power to the grid.“StandardX began with a problem: isotope supply limited by legacy infrastructure. This raise moves us from concept into engineering, physics into hardware, and conversations into delivery,” said Ross Allen, CTO StandardX. “Our immediate priority is our industrial site in London, where we will deploy our first isotope refinery system and work closely with clinicians and researchers to start building a reliable supply chain.”The £10m seed round is led by European deep tech investors Vsquared Ventures and East X Ventures, who have backed some of Europe’s most successful deep tech pioneers.“Radiopharma is approaching an extraordinary inflection point, but isotope supply simply hasn’t kept pace,” said Lise Rechsteiner, General Partner at Vsquared.“StandardX is building a fundamentally flexible production platform that can move with the science, from the isotopes medicine needs today to those that will define the next generation of cancer treatment. We believe it can become critical infrastructure for the next era of radiopharma and Richard and Ross have the rare technical expertise and ambition to build it. Being located in London puts StandardX at the heart of one of Europe’s leading ecosystems for cancer research and clinical trials.”

title: Geared turbofan jet engine to boost 5,400-mile range jet's thrust
content: A US-based aerospace equipment producer has reportedly delivered the first aircraft powered by its brand new GTF Advantage turbofan engine, which offers up to twice the time on wing and up to 8 percent more takeoff thrust.Connecticut-based Pratt & Whitney, an RTX business, announced on September 24 that its GTF Advantage engine has entered service aboard an Airbus A321XLR delivered to United Airlines. It is expected to bring greater efficiency to the whole A320neo family.According to RTX, a global manufacturer of aerospace and defense systems that was formerly known as Raytheon Technologies, the jet engine will offer greater durability, more thrust, and longer-range capability aboard the Airbus A321XLR.The A321XLR is a long-range single-aisle jet that can fly up to 5,400 miles (8,700 kilometers). It is built to link destinations that were previously difficult to reach with single-aisle jets. “The first delivery of a GTF Advantage-powered aircraft to United Airlines signifies a new chapter in our relationship that spans nearly a century,” Rick Deurloo, Pratt & Whitney commercial engines president, stated. Improved engine durabilityDeurloo said that the new engine delivers between four and eight percent more takeoff thrust than the current GTF model. According to the manufacturer, the additional power helps enable longer-range operations. United is the first airline to get an aircraft with the novel engine standard. The GTF Advantage is also more durable and can deliver up to twice the time on wing. This refers to how long an engine can operate before it needs maintenance.The Pratt & Whitney GTF Advantage engine.Credit: RTXAt the same time, the GTF Advantage features what the company describes as the most advanced hot section in the single-aisle aircraft market. The hot section has parts exposed to some of the highest temperatures inside a jet engine.Despite the changes, the GTF Advantage remains compatible with the current GTF engine. This could simplify operations for carriers that operate aircraft with both engine standards. Pratt & Whitney aims to transition its entire PW1100G-JM production line to the GTF Advantage specification by 2028.“GTF-powered aircraft are helping us reduce fuel burn and improve reliability as we add new destinations around the world for our customers,” Ankit Gupta, United Airlines senior VP and chief air operations officer, added. Updating the existing fleetRTX revealed that operators of existing GTF engines will also have access to some of the durability improvements. Pratt & Whitney plans to offer its GTF Hot Section Plus, or HS+, upgrade for the current PW1100G-JM engine.According to the firm, the upgrade will allow existing engines to reach up to 90-95 percent of the durability benefits offered by the GTF Advantage. Meanwhile, the HS+ option is set to become available for installation during maintenance visits early next year.The engine the first in a new line that builds on the baseline GTF engine.Credit: RTX“We are excited to welcome Pratt & Whitney’s newest GTF engine to our fleet,” Gupta concluded in a press release. “Pratt & Whitney has been a key supplier for United Airlines throughout our long, shared history, powering multiple United aircraft types.”Pratt & Whitney has been developing aircraft propulsion technologies since 1925. The company currently supports more than 90,000 engines worldwide through its maintenance, repair, and overhaul network.

title: 3-mm implants use body tissue to send signals without Bluetooth
content: Georgia Tech engineers have developed a wireless networking system that lets tiny implants communicate through body tissue, potentially allowing sensors in one part of the body to trigger treatment somewhere else.The Smart Wireless Autonomous Networking System, or SWANS, uses the body’s natural ionic conductivity to transmit electrical signals between implanted and wearable devices. The approach avoids conventional wireless technologies such as Bluetooth and near-field communication, which can struggle to transmit signals through human tissue.The low-power technology allowed the researchers to build implants smaller than 3 millimeters, making them small enough to be delivered using a syringe rather than requiring surgery. The devices can communicate with other implants as well as an external wearable hub.Researchers demonstrated the system in rats by creating a network linking sensors and neural interfaces across the body. When a sensor detected movement in a rat’s front paw, another device was automatically activated to stimulate a hind-leg muscle, producing a contraction that mimicked part of the animal’s natural walking motion.Body becomes the networkSWANS works by sending electrical pulses through surrounding tissue. Each implant can be programmed to recognize pulses with specific voltages and durations, allowing the network to selectively activate individual devices.The system could therefore separate where a biological signal is detected from where treatment is delivered.“With our system, you can now place sensors in the best possible place to detect a biological signal and place actuators in the best possible place to perform a therapeutic action,” said Alex Abramson, the study’s senior author and an assistant professor at Georgia Tech.“They don’t need to be connected, aligned, or even near each other; they can just send signals to each other through the surrounding tissue.”Traditional wireless systems present challenges for very small implants because their antennas and power requirements can increase device size. SWANS instead relies on the conductivity of biological tissue to carry its signals, reducing the hardware and energy required for communication.The implants use passive electronic components that consume essentially no power while waiting for a signal. They activate when triggered and can then perform a programmed action.Tiny implants coordinate treatmentThe researchers estimate that a small actuator activated once per day could operate for about a year before requiring replacement. Tests also found that the electrical pulses used for communication did not damage tissue samples.SWANS is not designed to move large quantities of information. Instead, implants exchange simple signals, such as whether a particular condition has been detected or whether an action should be triggered.More demanding data processing can take place on an external wearable hub. The hub can combine readings from multiple implants and coordinate therapeutic responses from devices elsewhere in the body.That architecture could eventually enable networks in which sensors monitor biological conditions continuously and automatically activate treatments when needed. Potential applications include neural stimulation and drug delivery, although the technology remains at the research stage.The researchers also demonstrated communication across different parts of the body, including devices positioned deep inside the stomach.“Our ultimate hope is to be able to fully automate human health — to be able to deliver a therapy exactly when it’s needed, where it’s needed, and to do so in a coordinated fashion across the body,” Abramson said.The study was published in the journal Science.

title: eFlyer 2 all-electric aircraft takes first flight with 80% lower costs
content: Bye Aerospace has put its eFlyer 2 into the air for the first time, opening the flight-test campaign for an all-electric aircraft aimed at U.S. pilot training. The Colorado-based company says the aircraft could cut operating costs by as much as 80 percent while producing no in-flight emissions.Chief Test Pilot Elliot Seguin flew the aircraft through its planned test profile from Centennial Airport near Denver. Engineers used the flight to gather early data on handling, aerodynamics, and propulsion performance.The first flight now gives Bye Aerospace a working aircraft for the next stage of development. It also moves the eFlyer 2 closer to FAA certification and eventual customer deliveries.Electric aircraft enters testingThe eFlyer 2 pairs an electric propulsion system with a lightweight composite airframe. Its design targets the economics of flight training, where fuel and maintenance can make every flight expensive.Bye Aerospace says the aircraft can reduce operating costs by up to 80 percent. That figure could become important for U.S. flight schools facing high training costs and pressure to keep aircraft flying. The aircraft also removes combustion emissions during flight. Its electric architecture could help operators reduce their exposure to volatile aviation fuel prices.Rod Zastrow, CEO of Bye Aerospace, said the first flight delivered strong results across several areas. “The first flight of eFlyer 2 exceeded all our expectations,” Zastrow said. He cited the aircraft’s aerodynamics, handling, and propulsion performance. The flight also recorded no maintenance discrepancies, according to the company.Designed around pilot trainingFlight schools represent the primary market for the eFlyer 2. Bye Aerospace also expects interest from air taxi operators and private owners.Pilot training creates a particularly demanding environment for aircraft. Students need predictable handling, while operators need high availability and manageable maintenance costs.The eFlyer 2 seeks to address both requirements through its electric powertrain and lightweight structure. Bye Aerospace also designed the aircraft around safety and repeatable handling for student pilots.Seguin said the aircraft handled well during the first flight. He added that the test validated years of engineering and ground testing.The program arrives as aviation faces persistent demand for new pilots. Lower operating costs could give training organizations more flexibility as they build flight hours for students.FAA certification work beginsThe first flight marks the beginning of a broader flight-test program. Bye Aerospace plans to progressively expand the aircraft’s flight envelope as testing continues.Engineers will collect additional performance data during those flights. The results will help establish the handling characteristics required for certification and training operations.The eFlyer 2 also brings together components from a broad aerospace supply chain. Suppliers include Safran Electrical and Power, magniX, Siemens, Toray, Garmin and Sensenich Propeller.Other partners include Composite Approach, Electro.Aero, Flying S, M4 Engineering, ACME Aero and Risse Racing. Their systems and components contribute to the aircraft’s electric propulsion, avionics, structure, and other functions.The next phase will test the aircraft across increasingly demanding conditions. Each flight should add data needed to support the FAA certification process.

title: 256-qubit quantum computer to power research at Florida university
content: US quantum computing company IonQ will install a 256-qubit trapped-ion quantum computer at Florida International University, giving researchers and students direct access to its sixth-generation quantum hardware.The Superion system is expected to be installed at FIU in Miami in late 2027 after the university completes a specialized on-campus data center. It will be the first Superion 256 system sold and deployed in Florida.The machine will use 256 physical trapped-ion qubits and support research spanning materials science, cybersecurity, health, logistics, artificial intelligence and power grid management. Faculty, students, visiting researchers and affiliated research centers will have access to the system.The agreement also makes FIU IonQ’s flagship academic partner in Florida, with the university planning to use the system for quantum research, education and workforce development across the region.Quantum hardware comes campus“This key partnership with Florida International University represents a major milestone in expanding direct physical access to IonQ’s industry-leading, high-performance quantum hardware,” said Niccolo de Masi, chairman and CEO of IonQ.“By housing our Superion 256 system directly on campus, FIU will lead the region in quantum research and training.”Unlike quantum systems accessed exclusively through cloud platforms, the agreement will place the hardware physically at FIU. Researchers will therefore have direct access to the university-based system for developing and running quantum computing workloads.IonQ’s Superion uses trapped-ion technology, in which electrically charged atoms are isolated and manipulated to serve as qubits. Such systems use electromagnetic fields to hold ions in place and lasers to control their quantum states and perform computational operations.FIU President Jeanette M. Nuñez said the system would provide the university’s researchers and students with direct access to advanced quantum computing infrastructure.“Having this 256-qubit quantum computer right on campus positions FIU researchers at the forefront of national quantum innovation,” Nuñez said.Research meets quantum trainingThe university expects the system to support both research and training. FIU has about 56,000 students and 1,200 faculty members, while regional industry partners are also expected to gain access through the initiative.Researchers could use the machine to investigate computational problems in areas ranging from materials and healthcare to cybersecurity and energy infrastructure.“The 256 physical qubits system located in Miami will enable our team to run complex computational workflows,” said Andres G. Gil, FIU senior vice president for research and economic development.FIU also plans to develop quantum computing curricula, degree programs and certificates while working with industry partners in South Florida and elsewhere.The university maintains a research showcase and briefing center in Washington, D.C., which could also help connect the program with federal agencies pursuing quantum technology initiatives.For IonQ, the deal expands physical deployment of its quantum hardware beyond cloud access. The Maryland-based company provides quantum computing systems and also develops technologies across quantum networking, sensing and security.Installation remains more than a year away, however, and depends on completion of FIU’s planned data center. Once installed, the 256-qubit machine is expected to serve as a regional hub for quantum research and training.

title: New fiber-based system raises $7M to extract uranium from seawater
content: Fluxnium has raised $7 million to develop a technology that could recover uranium directly from seawater. The startup says its approach could create a new domestic source for the U.S. nuclear industry.Congruent Ventures led the seed round, with participation from Constellation Technology Ventures and Active Impact Investments. Fluxnium will use the funding for technology development, pilot testing, and scale-up.The company is developing a specialized fiber that captures dissolved uranium as seawater flows across its surface. Fluxnium developed the material with a U.S. national laboratory.The approach targets a difficult engineering problem. Oceans contain enormous quantities of uranium, but the element exists at extremely low concentrations.Fiber targets ocean uraniumSeawater contains an estimated 4.5 billion metric tons of uranium. That resource dwarfs currently identified deposits on land.Extracting it economically remains difficult because uranium atoms are spread across vast volumes of water. Fluxnium’s system focuses on capturing those atoms without pumping seawater through a large processing facility.Its fiber provides a large surface area for uranium adsorption. The material can sit inside longline systems deployed in open water.Fluxnium modeled the infrastructure on marine farming systems. Seaweed and mussel operations already use similar longline structures in offshore environments.Operators would retrieve the fiber after it collects uranium. Processing would then recover the uranium before crews redeploy the material.That cycle could allow production capacity to grow through additional fiber deployment. It could also avoid the lengthy development process associated with opening new uranium mines.U.S. nuclear fuel supplyThe technology arrives as the United States looks to strengthen its nuclear fuel supply chain. Fluxnium says the country currently imports more than 90% of its uranium.Jeff Green, Fluxnium’s CEO and founder, said rising electricity demand could increase pressure on nuclear fuel supplies.“Fluxnium is developing a new domestic and sustainable supply of uranium,” Green said. He pointed to offshore infrastructure as a potential path toward competitive production.The company also argues that seawater extraction could avoid some impacts associated with conventional uranium mining. Those include mine tailings and groundwater concerns.Economic performance will remain a major test for the technology. Fluxnium says its projected costs could compete with conventional uranium mining.Constellation sees the technology as another potential option for future nuclear fuel supplies. Jason Murphy, its vice president of nuclear fuels, said new domestic uranium sources could support growing nuclear demand.Scaling offshore systemFluxnium now needs to demonstrate that its laboratory-developed material can perform reliably at larger scales. Offshore deployment introduces engineering challenges beyond simply capturing uranium.The fiber must operate in seawater while surviving marine conditions. Engineers must also develop practical methods for retrieval, processing, and redeployment.Fluxnium’s seed funding will support that next stage. The company says its system could expand output by adding more collection infrastructure.That model could give uranium production a different path to expansion. Instead of developing another mine, operators could add more offshore collection capacity.The concept remains under development, however. Commercial viability will depend on extraction rates, material durability, processing costs, and performance at pilot scale.

title: US advances nuclear fuel plant with 5-metric-ton uranium capacity
content: X-energy has completed the main structure of a new U.S. facility designed to manufacture advanced nuclear fuel for small modular reactors, moving the project toward equipment installation and commercial production.The 214,000-square-foot TX-1 facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, is being developed by TRISO-X, a wholly owned subsidiary of X-energy. The company said completing vertical construction clears the way for interior work, installation of fuel fabrication equipment and construction of supporting facilities.Once operational, TX-1 is expected to manufacture about 700,000 TRISO fuel pebbles each year, using roughly 5 metric tons of uranium. That output would be enough to supply as many as 11 of X-energy’s Xe-100 advanced reactors.The project is expected to become the first new commercial-scale advanced nuclear fuel fabrication facility built in the U.S. in more than 50 years. Earlier this year, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission granted the plant a 40-year Special Nuclear Material License, which X-energy says is the first NRC Category 2 fuel fabrication license for processing high-assay low-enriched uranium, or HALEU.Fuel plant takes shape“Completing vertical construction is a major milestone for TX-1 and another tangible demonstration of the progress our team is making in Oak Ridge,” said Joel Duling, president of TRISO-X.“We are moving from constructing the core and shell of the facility to building out the interior utilities, installing manufacturing equipment, and constructing key support capabilities.”Clark Construction Group is handling construction and will now focus on the process equipment and administration building, fuel manufacturing equipment and an adjacent graphite matrix powder building.TRISO, or tristructural isotropic fuel, consists of tiny uranium fuel particles surrounded by multiple layers of carbon- and ceramic-based materials. These coatings are designed to contain fission products and allow the fuel to tolerate temperatures considerably higher than conventional nuclear fuel.X-energy’s Xe-100 is a high-temperature gas-cooled small modular reactor designed around TRISO fuel. Each reactor module is designed to produce 80 megawatts of electricity, with four modules forming a standard 320-megawatt plant.Reactors drive fuel demandTX-1 is initially intended to supply fuel for X-energy’s planned Xe-100 deployment at Dow’s UCC Seadrift Operations manufacturing site in Texas. The project is being advanced through the U.S. Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program.The company is also pursuing Xe-100 projects with Energy Northwest, Amazon and Centrica, creating a potential future market for fuel produced at the Oak Ridge facility.TRISO-X has meanwhile expanded its Oak Ridge nuclear fuel campus by about 70 acres and extended its research partnership with Oak Ridge National Laboratory. It has also started construction of TX-L, a separate research and development facility.Finishing the building’s main structure does not mean TX-1 is ready to manufacture fuel. The company must now complete its interior systems, install and commission specialized production equipment and prepare the facility for commercial operations.For X-energy, bringing TX-1 online would establish a domestic manufacturing source for the specialized fuel needed to support deployment of its planned Xe-100 reactor fleet.
